title: Ed Oliver is now the fourth-longest tenured Buffalo Bills player
summary: That headline should serve as a stark reminder of the speed at which time flies in the NFL. After the firing of nine-year head coach Sean McDermott, the construction of a revamped coaching staff, the Buffalo Bills first-round pick from 2019, Ed Oliver, is now the fourth-longest tenured player on the roster. Can you list […]
full_text: ORCHARD PARK, NEW YORK - DECEMBER 31: Ed Oliver #91 of the Buffalo Bills celebrates a first quarter sack during a game against the New England Patriots at Highmark Stadium on December 31, 2023 in Orchard Park, New York. (Photo by Timothy T Ludwig/Getty Images) | Getty Images That headline should serve as a stark reminder of the speed at which time flies in the NFL. After the firing of nine-year head coach Sean McDermott, the construction of a revamped coaching staff, the Buffalo Bills first-round pick from 2019, Ed Oliver, is now the fourth-longest tenured player on the roster. Can you list the three-longest tenured Bills? Third-longest is Josh Allen (2018, first round) Second-longest is Dion Dawkins (2017, second round) And the longest-tenured Bills player is long snapper Reid Ferguson, now 32, who joined the Bills as an undrafted free agent out of LSU after the 2016 NFL Draft. Heck, when Ferguson takes the field in Week 1, he will be playing for his third Bills head coach (Rex Ryan, McDermott, and now Joe Brady). Here’s a graphic to demonstrate: Hats off to Dawson Knox too… the fifth-longest tenured member of the Bills entering the 2026 season. One of the indisputable characteristics of the McDermott era was the coach’s unwavering reliance on familiar players regardless of age or amount of stops outside of Buffalo — think Jordan Phillips, Baylon Spector, A.J. Klein, Deane Marlowe, Matt Milano, Jordan Poyer, Shaq Thompson, Tre’Davious White, Shaq Lawson, Gabe Davis etc. Because of that, the 2025 Bills were relatively well-represented by players acquired in some way, shape, or form during the 2016 and 2017 offseasons. And many of those players were placed in key roles, in key games. Now, when Oliver steps on the grass at the new Highmark Stadium, he will be the longest-tenured Buffalo defender by two whole years over Greg Rousseau. I don’t know if Oliver has reached “Unc” status yet. But his inching his way toward it. Another indication of the Bills massive roster churning over the past few months — Rousseau, who only turned 26 in April, is the team’s seventh-longest tenured player.

full_text: Ohio State Buckeyes cornerback Davison Igbinosun (1) celebrates an interception during the first half of the Big Ten Conference championship game against the Indiana Hoosiers at Lucas Oil Stadium in Indianapolis on Dec. 6, 2025. | Adam Cairns/Columbus Dispatch / USA TODAY NETWORK via Imagn Images Buffalo Bills training camp begins next week… what a fantastic sentence to write after the prolonged time spent away from football. There’s second-round pick T.J. Parker… could he give quarterbacks problems all season and come close to double digit sacks? We do know Parker has been training this offseason with veteran Bradley Chubb who signed with the Bills in free agency. Not a bad mentor to have as a rookie. Cornerback Davison Igbinosun was the pick after Parker and again is a question mark in this draft class that could provide a huge impact. title: Buffalo Bills 2026 scouting report: outside linebacker Michael Hoecht
summary: The Buffalo Bills have searched for years to find the best combination of pass rushers that they can acquire. General manager Brandon Beane has tinkered with the defensive line multiple times throughout his tenure, pouring tremendous resources into the position over the last decade. Have the Bills found a combination that works? I’d vote no, […]
full_text: ORCHARD PARK, NEW YORK - JUNE 9: Michael Hoecht #55 congratulates Cade Denhoff #57 with a headbutt during the Buffalo Bills mandatory minicamp at Kaleida Health Performance Center on June 9, 2026 in Orchard Park, New York. (Photo by Joe Hrycych/Getty Images) | Getty Images The Buffalo Bills have searched for years to find the best combination of pass rushers that they can acquire. General manager Brandon Beane has tinkered with the defensive line multiple times throughout his tenure, pouring tremendous resources into the position over the last decade. Have the Bills found a combination that works? I’d vote no, as they continuously seem to be searching for that golden goose at edge rusher who can consistently harrass opposing quarterbacks without the need for a blitz. That doesn’t mean that every signing Beane has made has been poor, as some of those acquisitions were derailed less by the player’s inability to perform and more by unfortunate injuries. Think Von Miller as one possible example. In today’s installment of “91 players in 91 days,” we discuss another pass-rusher whose first year with the team was derailed by a major injury. _____________________________________________________________________________ Name: Michael Hoecht Number: 55 Position: OLB Height/Weight: 6’4” 264 lbs. Age: 28 (29 on 10/5/2026) Experience/Draft: 6; signed with the Los Angeles Rams following the 2020 NFL Draft College: Brown Acquired: Signed with Buffalo on 3/14/2025 Financial situation (per Spotrac): Hoecht enters the second year of the three-year, $21 million contract he signed prior to last season. If he’s on the 53-man roster, Hoecht’s 2026 cap hit is $7,019,647. If Buffalo released him, they’re on the hook for a dead cap charge of $9,318,588. 2025 Recap: Hoecht’s year was cursed from the beginning, as he spent the first six games suspended as a result of a positive PED test. Buffalo knew that the suspension was coming, as Hoecht was forthcoming about it, and they signed him anyway. Hoecht played in all three of Buffalo’s preseason games and was extremely impactful, notching five tackles, one pass knockdown, one tackle for loss, and one sack in those three games. His season debut was highly anticipated, and he did not disappoint upon playing in regular season games. He totaled three tackles, 1.5 sacks, one tackle for loss, and one quarterback hit on 40 defensive snaps in Buffalo’s 40-14 drubbing of the Carolina Panthers. The following week, Hoecht had two tackles and half a sack in a 28-21 victory over the Kansas City Chiefs. However, he played just 24 defensive snaps thanks to an injury, which we quickly learned was a torn Achilles that caused Hoecht to miss the remainder of the season. He was mic’d up for the Chiefs’ contest, and he chose to stay on the bench after his injury rather than watch the rest of the game from the locker room. Positional outlook: Hoecht is one of eight outside linebackers on the current roster. Greg Rousseau, Bradley Chubb, T.J. Parker, Javon Solomon, Cade Denhoff, Mike Danna, and Andre Jones Jr. are the others. 2026 Offseason: Hoecht has been rehabbing his Achilles injury with the goal of playing Week One in mind. He has said that he really wants to be ready for training camp , as well, but he knows that the top priority is to be ready to play as soon as possible. He has been spotted sprinting in workouts and working with resistance bands throughout offseason workouts. 2026 Season outlook: While injuries to Jordan Poyer, Maxwell Hairston, and Terrel Bernard were felt in the immediate during the postseason, there’s an argument to be made that no injury impacted Buffalo’s defense more than Hoecht’s, as the immediate boost to the team’s pass rush that he provided was clear and obvious. Who knows what would have happened had his Achilles not torn during that win over the Chiefs. Perhaps the Bills would have picked up an extra win or two and made up the ground they needed on the New England Patriots in order to claim another AFC East crown. Could Hoecht have continued his breakneck pace over a larger sample size? We’ll never know, but hopefully, we’ll be able to see what his impact will be this season. Hoecht is a versatile player, as he was used in a variety of roles during his time with the Rams. Former head coach Sean McDermott and former defensive coordinator Bobby Babich deployed him in a few ways, as well, as he was used outside and inside, with his hand in the dirt and in a two-point stance. In new defensive coordinator Jim Leonhard’s defense, that versatility will certainly come in handy. In two seasons as an outside linebacker with the Rams prior to coming to Buffalo, Hoecht logged 137 tackles and nine sacks across 34 games, 22 of which were starts. He had 13 tackles and a sack in three playoff games, as well. What Hoecht does this season is likely tied to his availability, at least in the early going. Buffalo won’t want to rush him back, but they’ll definitely want to use him in some capacity as soon as his body allows them to do so. Hoecht stands to be one of Buffalo’s top edge rushers. There’s no doubt that he’s going to make the team. The question is how much can he do, and when can he do it. Hoecht is likely going to be a rotational piece, swapping in as a part of the top-four edge rushers with Rousseau, Chubb, and Parker. If he can provide even half of the juice he did last offseason, we’re looking at a seven-or-eight-sack pace. That would be fantastic for a Buffalo defense in desperate need of pass rush. Hoecht’s health is one of the big X-Factors for the team this season. If he’s healthy, he should wreak havoc in a good way.

title: Buffalo Rumblings Tailgate Series: Inside the inaugural Bills VIP tailgate
summary: For many members of Bills Mafia, the tailgate is just as important as the game itself. Not everyone has the luxury of hauling grills, tents, coolers, tables, and enough food to feed half a parking lot. Tens of thousands of Bills fans travel to Buffalo from across the country and even around the world every […]
full_text: Rendering of Bills VIP Tailgate For many members of Bills Mafia, the tailgate is just as important as the game itself. Not everyone has the luxury of hauling grills, tents, coolers, tables, and enough food to feed half a parking lot. Tens of thousands of Bills fans travel to Buffalo from across the country and even around the world every season. For them, organized tailgate experiences offer a chance to jump right into the atmosphere without worrying about packing equipment, or finding a place to set up. That’s exactly what this new series is all about. For me, the game day experience has become an important aspect of why I love attending games in Orchard Park. As I prepare for my 102nd consecutive Buffalo Bills game, home and away, I’ve been fortunate enough to experience many of the different tailgates that make Bills Mafia so unique. Some are free. Some are paid. Some are legendary Bills Mafia traditions. I’ll be highlighting the different tailgate experiences available throughout the 2026 season, breaking down where they’re located, what they cost, what’s included, and what kind of fan they’re designed for. We start with one of the newest additions to game day. The Bills VIP Tailgate Making its debut for the inaugural season at the new Highmark Stadium is the Bills VIP Tailgate, an all-inclusive premium pregame experience operated by Bullseye Event Group. Located directly across Abbott Road from the Toyota Gate E entrance, it is about as convenient as it gets. Guests can enjoy the festivities before simply walking across the street to enter the stadium. The event opens four hours before kickoff for every Buffalo Bills home game. What’s Included? Unlike a traditional parking lot tailgate, this experience is designed as an all-inclusive hospitality event. Admission includes: Unlimited premium food stations Open premium bar and bottled beer Pepsi products and non-alcoholic beverages Multiple bars Large LED screens showing NFL pregame coverage Live DJ Xbox gaming area Food is curated by Food Network celebrity chef Aaron May and features a rotating menu inspired by Buffalo favorites. Depending on the game, fans can expect barbecue, premium grilled selections, taco stations, Buffalo classics, shareable appetizers, desserts, salads, and more. Tickets The Bills VIP Tailgate is a ticketed event. Adult Admission: $135 Children (9-17): $70 Children 8 years old and younger are admitted free with a paying adult and do not require a ticket. Note: Parking and a game ticket are not included with regular admission. Tickets are available through Bullseye Event Group for each Buffalo Bills home game. Is There a Charity Component? BillsMafia is really amazing when it comes to charity and supporting the community. One unique feature of the Bills VIP tailgate is the live silent auction held during each tailgate, featuring signed Buffalo Bills memorabilia. Proceeds benefit charitable causes through Bullseye Event Group’s event partnerships, giving fans an opportunity to take home exclusive memorabilia while supporting a good cause. Who Is This Tailgate For? The Bills VIP Tailgate isn’t trying to replace the legendary parking lot culture that helped build Bills Mafia. Instead, it fills a different niche. If you’re flying into Buffalo for the weekend, driving in from across the state, coming by yourself, bringing clients, entertaining family, or simply want a stress-free game day where everything is taken care of, this may be exactly what you’re looking for. There’s no need to pack coolers, bring a grill, or spend hours setting up. Just show up, eat, drink, meet fellow Bills fans, and enjoy the atmosphere before making the short walk into the new Highmark Stadium. As the new stadium ushers in a new era of Buffalo Bills football, it’s only fitting that fans now have more ways than ever to experience game day. And this is just the beginning. Coming next in the Buffalo Rumblings Tailgate Series: we’ll head from the premium hospitality side of Bills Mafia to one of the fan-driven traditions that has made Buffalo tailgating legendary, proving that whether your budget is $0 or $135, there’s a place for every member of Bills Mafia before kickoff.

title: Brian Answers: Training camp answers to all your questions!
summary: Hello CSR! Welcome to Brian Answers, part two of your weekly Panthers fan mailbag for everyone! We’re into the heart of the preseason before the Preseason. Let’s talk! Revshawn: As the two time, back-to-back, champion of the LPL Financial C3 Fantasy Football league I wish you well in your coming battles Brian. I hope that […]
full_text: Jun 9, 2026; Charlotte, NC, USA; Carolina Panthers quarterback Bryce Young (9) looks downfield during the first day of mini camp at Bank of America Stadium practice facility. Mandatory Credit: Jim Dedmon-Imagn Images | Jim Dedmon-Imagn Images Hello CSR! Welcome to Brian Answers, part two of your weekly Panthers fan mailbag for everyone! We’re into the heart of the preseason before the Preseason. Let’s talk! Revshawn: As the two time, back-to-back, champion of the LPL Financial C3 Fantasy Football league I wish you well in your coming battles Brian. I hope that you crush all of your rivals and bring home the coveted Cat Scratch Reader Grand Champion trophy. A honor only bestowed upon the grandest of champions that outfought, outlasted, and outthunk their enemies. I appreciate the gesture, kind sir. I have three leagues; a bigger money fantasy league (1 QB, 2RB, TE, 2 WR, 2 WR/TE/RB flex, K, Def) league, a dynasty league, and a family 2 QB league. In my 1st league, I’ve been in it since 2018. Most points scored all time, been to the finals 4 times. 0-4. Hoping to get the championship this season. I’ll let you know if we lock it in this year! Dcangio09: What’s your Barometer for Bryce Young to get a worthwhile extension? Mine is a successful offense, winning team unless major injuries occur and minimum 7.0 YPA displaying actual NFL level production and efficiency as a passer compared to his historically low marks to date. I’m kind of in the same boat. I’d like to see him around the middle tier at least statistically in passing yards, yards per attempt, and touchdowns (though rushing TDs should be counted). I’m not expecting him to ever have a 2015 Cam Newton season, but when he’s on I think he’s solid enough to beat most teams in the NFL with some help. I want to see consistency and around 10-15 QB production before I’d ever consider an extension this off-season. We’ll see. Luckily, they don’t HAVE to make that decision this off-season. But a major statistical overhaul would make that decision a bit easier. Coach_K: There should be some good battles for positions this offseason; unlucky that practices will not be available to the public, lucky we got 4 preseason games. But there is one that keeps mentioned getting traded and he’s a Charlotte fave in Leggette. I don’t think our WR corps is legit enough, so I’m curious if we get another guy in (via trade?) or if Horn or Metchie steps up. I wouldn’t count on our tight ends to fill up that stat sheet. What is Leggette’s contract situation if he can’t find his footing? I think Xavier Legette gets every opportunity to take the WR3/4 spot this season. I think he’ll get mixed in a bit regardless of how much Chris Brazell plays. But if he continues to be in the same position he was in 2025, I don’t see Carolina re-signing him. He’s going to be safe next season just because he’s on a rookie deal, but this is the year to take a major step forward, if it’s ever coming. @WTMealey: Preseason watching mode? 1 screen-all in sound on engaged the whole time 2 screens sound on main screen and it has my attention, but if its a commercial or I get a notification phone is now the priority 3 screens-doing work/surfing on laptop phone face up for notifications and texts tv on but is kinda background noise unless there’s a score or turnover-sound low but barely loud enough to hear big plays It depends on the week for me. The first game of the preseason always keeps me engaged the whole time, or at least until the 4th quarter. I generally hit the “oh yeah, this is preseason” wall within a couple of drives, but I like to watch for players I’m impressed with anyway (Corey Thornton and Lathan Ransom as examples). I generally stay in the same neighborhood for the 2nd week, though its mostly just to post about observations on CSR’s social media accounts. By the 3rd game I’m very much just paying attention just because I have to, so several other screens are being used. schrodingersblackcat: Brian, what’s going through Greg Olsen’s head these days watching the guy who took his job play-pretend being a pro wrestler with the likes of Logan Paul? Greg’s a smart guy, I’m sure he’s appreciating the business Tom Brady is working (wrestling term for those not in the know) with Logan Paul. Nothing wrong with garnering interest in a public feud that will likely pay off with a “wrestling match” between two celebrities. SnarkyComet: I was watching a YT channel’s preview of the 2026 Panthers and they mentioned that we have the worst TE room in the league. But, taking our bias out of it, is that objectively true? Do we have the absolute worst TE unit in the league? Do you think we should possibly make a move for someone to strengthen that position before the season starts? If so, who would be a reasonable good fit for Canales/Idzick’s scheme? And who would be the odd man out? This iteration of the Panthers just doesn’t rely on tight ends as receivers as much as they have in the past. I think they all do a little bit of different things, which helps mitigate not having a Brock Bowers or George Kittle or Greg Olsen in the room. It might be the “worst” tight end room in the NFL, but I really don’t think that matters too much for what the Panthers do. They task them with blocking and Ja’Tavion Sanders fills that receiver specialist role. I think it made sense to invest elsewhere on this team and keep the room they have for the most part. So I’m not projecting any major signings at the position. positivebob: After being around DC’s camps for a couple of years, what kind of practices does he run? I know the routine changes and the intensity ramps up as they get closer to week 1, but in general does he run a physical camp, live tackling, full speed, lots of contact? More half speed, walk throughs? More individual drills, 7×7, situational football? Rookies and long shots get extended looks, how much do guys move between 1st, 2nd, 3rd teams? What does a DC TC look like? I didn’t want to ignore your question, but honestly I don’t have any better idea of what training camp looks like than any of you. The Panthers do seem to mix in guys they have conviction for with the first team (Jonathon Brooks already is getting reps with the first team). I haven’t seen anything substantial to think their camp is much different than your average NFL team though. I was a bit surprised that they declared OT Monroe Freeling the starting right tackle this early into training camp, so it seems they don’t stick to any one philosophy so much as just analyze the current roster and make calls based on that. Bull123: tough news about Moton…sounds like he is gonna be out for a while first off hope he is OK & makes a full recovery…blood clots you do not mess around with do you think Panthers have known this for a while?…signing BC is a result of this news? No idea how long Taylor Moton will be out, but the team has come up with a plan as mentioned above. I don’t think the Panthers knew this prior to June, and Brady Christensen hasn’t really ever been used at tackle since Dave Canales became the head coach that I can remember. I think he’s purely an interior lineman, but he has played at both tackle positions in the past. I don’t think signing him was a reaction to Moton’s diagnosis as much as just bringing in depth they already needed. dayneb12: I feel a good chunk of this year’s draft class has a chance to be starters at some point. Which rookies do you expect to start immediately and which do you expect will be starters before this season ends? Obviously, Monroe Freeling will end up starting at RT right away with the Moton news. I would expect DL Lee Hunter to be heavily involved early, especially if Bobby Brown’s injury turns out to be longer term. Beyond that, maybe C Sam Hecht will start right away but I am not holding my breath on that. I do think its possible Hecht and S Zakee Wheatley could be starting by the end of the season. CB Will Lee could also be a starter if…

title: 2026 Season Opener Countdown: 51 Days Remaining
summary: Here at Cat Scratch Reader we have counted down the final 100 days leading up to the Carolina Panthers season opener by for at least the past ten years. We’ve always done this by highlighting the current player on the roster whose jersey number matches the day on the countdown. This year, we decided to […]
full_text: CHARLOTTE, NC - NOVEMBER 13: Geoff Hangartner #63 of the Carolina Panthers provides pass protection for Cam Newton #1 during fourth quarter action against the Tennessee Titans at Bank of America Stadium on November 13, 2011 in Charlotte, North Carolina. The Titans defeated the Panthers 30-3. (Photo by Brian A. Westerholt/Getty Images) | Getty Images Here at Cat Scratch Reader we have counted down the final 100 days leading up to the Carolina Panthers season opener by for at least the past ten years. We’ve always done this by highlighting the current player on the roster whose jersey number matches the day on the countdown. This year, we decided to change that up a bit by counting down our own list of the Top 100 Panthers of all time. This does not correspond to jersey number, does not need to be somebody who wore a jersey, and will in no way be controversial. #51. Geoff Hangartner Geoff Hangartner is about as offensive lineman as they come. He played college football at Texas A&M, where he never missed a game, though he did get in trouble for drinking in driving. He was picked by the Panthers in the fifth round in 2004 and took a role as a backup center and special teams player. He was thrust into a starting role in year two due to injury and played well. Still, he was demoted back to a bench role for year three and was only called upon when injuries hit. He split time as a starter and reserve in his fourth season before departing for Buffalo in free agency in 2009. The Panthers apparently realized what they had and re-signed Hangartner after the Bills let him go in order to go younger on the offensive line. He slid in at right tackle and was an integral part of a strong offensive line that helped Cam Newton win rookie of the year honors. He seemed poised to hold down that spot for a while but went from starting guard to training camp cut before the 2013 season, once again as the victim of a team making a youth push on the offensive line. He ended up making a few cameos as an injury replacement that season before retiring. Hangartner was the quintessential underappreciated interior lineman that never wowed anyone but also more than held is own. It seemed like he was always a target for replacement, but he always showed up and played well whenever the team was forced to rely on him. And he was a passable kickoff returner in a pinch. He returned three kickoffs during the 2007 season, one of which set up a game winning drive against the Seahawks. Not bad for a 300 pounder.

title: WCG Dynasty Fantasy Football: Assessing Jeff Berckes’ Roster
summary: We have five teams left for our series of WCG Dynasty Fantasy Football roster assessments. Today we are looking at Jeff Berckes’ roster. JB took over this roster this past offseason and is working on retooling it and tweaking it into his image. Is this roster ready to win now? Does it need to rebuild? […]
full_text: BALTIMORE, MARYLAND - OCTOBER 26: Dayo Odeyingbo #55 of the Chicago Bears looks on during the national anthem prior to an NFL football game against the Baltimore Ravens at M&T Bank Stadium on October 26, 2025 in Baltimore, Maryland. (Photo by Michael Owens/Getty Images) | Getty Images We have five teams left for our series of WCG Dynasty Fantasy Football roster assessments. Today we are looking at Jeff Berckes’ roster. JB took over this roster this past offseason and is working on retooling it and tweaking it into his image. Is this roster ready to win now? Does it need to rebuild? Let’s take a look at the roster and see how it looks: Let’s start with the offense, and let’s start in the QB room. There’s not an issue here. Have to love Joe Burrow as a QB1, and Cam Ward as a developmental guy, and your QB2 absolutely works. As for Watson? I don’t think he’s got anything left in the tank, but he 100% deserves a roster spot, so it is what it is there. JB may have every running back in the league. A dozen backs on the roster, if healthy, Hampton and Skattebo should be a solid starting duo, and there is some decent depth behind them. There’s a handful of dart throws on here as well, but July and August are the time for RB dart throws to see how things look on depth charts come Labor Day. There’s plenty of talent in the WR room, but there aren’t enough players behind the top talent. JSN, Nabers, London, and Rice, if healthy, are a fabulous WR foursome; Lemon is in a nice spot to develop behind that group, Bateman is always a decent spot start, and Flournoy might have a nice season this year. If the big 4 have any injuries, I worry there aren’t enough players behind them to keep the team afloat. I don’t see much in the tight end room, but it should be functional. Mark Andrews should be getting plenty of targets after Likely and Kolar have left and Dulcich and Strange score some points from time to time. There’s no upside here, and there’s more downside, but most likely this is a functional room, nothing more, nothing less. On the defensive side of the ball, we will find some holes. The DT room doesn’t have a lot of scorers. Can Togai repeat last year’s performance? Or was it a bit of a fluke? There’s a lot of talk that his reps will go down this year. Robinson is always decent, but he’s 31. I’m not the biggest believer in Orhorhoro, but if he takes a step forward, that would help the room a lot. The edge room certainly needs help. Will David Bailey be an impact rookie? JB certainly hopes so. I haven’t given up on Chop Robinson, although perhaps I should. Beyond that, it’s just a lot of rotational players and not much upside. The LB room has some solid scorers from last year, and he adds Reese into the mix. Gray looks like he should have several years of scoring points; Davis obviously doesn’t have much left, but Bolton and Walker do a good job compiling points. This room looks to be okay. I like Sainristil as a point scorer at CB; I don’t see too much of a reason for many of the other CBs on the roster. The safety room is anchored by Emmanwori, which looks great; it could use a handful of stronger safeties beyond that, but it’s decent. The taxi squad has some talent. Washington, Sarratt, and Raridon are perfect guys to place there, and if Lawrence can have a big rookie season, that would certainly help the edge room. If JB gets through the season relatively unscathed, I think this team is a playoff team. It has a pretty solid starting lineup; the issue is if there are a few injuries here. This team doesn’t have depth at many different positions, and if JB struggles with injuries, his team is going to find itself drafting in the top 5.

title: WCG Dynasty Fantasy Football: Assessing Bill Zimmerman’s Roster
summary: We have six more rosters to analyze before training camp officially opens for the Chicago Bears, so let’s get into it with two today, two Saturday, and two on Sunday. Today we are going to look at my roster and see where it’s at. A couple of years ago, I decided to rip my team […]
full_text: LAKE FOREST, ILLINOIS - JUNE 3: Dillon Thieneman #31 of the Chicago Bears looks on during a Chicago Bears OTA Offseason Workout at Halas Hall on June 3, 2026 in Lake Forest, Illinois. (Photo by Geoff Stellfox/Getty Images) | Getty Images We have six more rosters to analyze before training camp officially opens for the Chicago Bears, so let’s get into it with two today, two Saturday, and two on Sunday. Today we are going to look at my roster and see where it’s at. A couple of years ago, I decided to rip my team to shreds and rebuild from the ground up completely through the draft. It’s been a fun, yet difficult exercise, and the team is starting to come into form, but it’s been multiple seasons of seriously losing records. My team was dominant early in this league, going to the first four title games and winning two of them. The team began to age and was barely clinging to being a playoff team. In year six, I made the playoffs as the last seed and went on a Cinderella run to win my 3rd title. I thought the timing was perfect to start fresh. I traded every player on my roster, literally every single one. I acquired a huge amount of draft capital over several years and have been working towards putting together what I hope is a young, dominant core that can eventually dominate, but we aren’t there yet. Let’s take a look at the roster: Let’s break down the roster, starting with the QB room. This room might be in excellent shape, or it might be a disaster. Will Jayden Daniels’ 2025 season be the norm, or will it be 2024? Will Michael Penix figure it out? Is Tyler Shough on his way to becoming a legit NFL QB, or did he just have a handful of good games? We will learn a lot about this room this season and see if it’s on strong footing or if it’s problematic. The running back room has had some misses. Johnathan Brooks’ injury was crippling to this room, and Kaleb Johnson, as of right now, appears to be an epic bust. RJ Harvey was pretty good last year but seems like he’s going to be losing carries, not gaining them. Can Jeremiyah Love stabilize this room? There are some other young backs that might be able to become contributors, but it’s still more wait and see here. The WR room is slowly coming together. Tet McMillan had a nice rookie season, and Alec Pierce appears to be on his way. Can Marvin Harrison Jr become the force we all expected him to be? If he’s a miss, that’s a crushing blow to the rebuild. Keon Coleman certainly hasn’t helped either. There are a few other decent young pieces here but not too many with high-end regular starter capabilities. The tight end room already might be the best one in the league. Brock Bowers is a force. Gadsen looks like the real deal, and Dalton Kincaid and Mason Taylor as TE3 and TE4 is certainly some decent depth. Moving over to the defensive side of the ball, the DT room has a nice starting duo of Murphy and Kancey, and Newton has shown some skills as well. Will Aaron Donald come back? If so, that certainly raises the bar in this room as well. In the edge room, Verse is already showing to be a legit fantasy threat; hopefully he won’t draw too much attention in Cleveland. Can Carter and/or Green become legit Edges that score points? If so, this room should settle in nicely, but if they struggle, it’ll be looking for a second-every-week starter. The linebacker room has a hilarious amount of players in it currently, but I do love me some linebackers. I love both Hill and Allen as rookies, and Cooper, Jihaad Campbell, and Jack Campbell all look the part. You can only start 4, so I will certainly be looking to make some trades here as we approach the season. At CB, I’m hoping I have the cheat code. We accumulate all stats for players, so if Hunter is a full-time CB and plays WR part-time, he will get points for both as a starting CB. If he can grab the usual 10 or 11 points from a CB and throw in 6 or 7 offensive points a game, Hunter could score up near 20 points a game, which will lap the competition. We will see if it comes together for him. The safety room is in solid shape right now. It has some young players who are already capable of starting and a couple of developmental guys as well, plus both Bears safeties to boot. The taxi squad is fairly talented as they go at this point in the season. Green is a dart throw; if the Giants don’t get healthy at WR, Fields might see time this year, Moore could be a useful piece in Detroit, Elarms-Orr has already been rumored to push for a starting job, and Haulcy has a pretty good chance to be decent in Indy’s defensive scheme. I’m curious to see how this team comes together this year. I think it has a shot at the playoffs, but I think it might fall short again. But if Jayden Daniels plays like 2024, Love and one of the other RBs become consistent point scorers, and if Harrison takes a step forward, this team could be really strong this year. The defense should score points; it’s just a matter of finding the right combination of players on offense.
author: Bill Zimmerman

title: Why the Bears will be watching Devon Witherspoon, Christian Gonzalez contracts closely
summary: Like it or not, there’s no escaping the business of sports. And even as the Chicago Bears prepare to open the 2026 NFL season with Super Bowl aspirations, one very important player has major question marks about their future with the franchise that could be illuminated soon. All-Pro cornerback Jaylon Johnson, who seems to be […]
full_text: Nov 28, 2025; Philadelphia, Pennsylvania, USA; Chicago Bears cornerback Jaylon Johnson (1) lines up for a play against the Philadelphia Eagles during the second quarter of the game at Lincoln Financial Field. Mandatory Credit: Eric Hartline-Imagn Images | Eric Hartline-Imagn Images Like it or not, there’s no escaping the business of sports. And even as the Chicago Bears prepare to open the 2026 NFL season with Super Bowl aspirations, one very important player has major question marks about their future with the franchise that could be illuminated soon. All-Pro cornerback Jaylon Johnson, who seems to be healthy and ready to roll this year after a groin injury hampered him in 2025, is now in the second half of a four-year, $76 million contract signed back in 2024. That means he’ll be looking for new money soon—potentially the last big payday of his career. Fortunately for him—perhaps less so for the Bears—a few elite defensive backs are about to set the terms of engagement for Johnson’s upcoming contract discussions. Seattle Seahawks cornerback Devon Witherspoon and New England Patriots corner Christian Gonzalez—both of whom came out of the 2023 NFL Draft—are each talking contract extensions with their current teams heading into their fourth NFL seasons, though in different stages. The Seahawks, it seems, are already willing to pay Witherspoon, one of the best all-around players at the position, north of $31 million a year, likely making him the highest-paid corner in the league. At least, that is, until the Patriots match or exceed that mark to retain Gonzalez, one of the best pure cover corners in football. With Houston’s Derek Stingley and Indianapolis’ Sauce Gardner averaging about $30 million after inking new deals last season, the top of the market is set for top cornerbacks. No doubt, Johnson will want in on that level of compensation. Though Johnson is older than all of those players, he’s still young enough at age 27 to merit a handsome payday. (Don’t forget that, at a similar age, the Bears inked DJ Moore to a long-term deal—four years, $110 million—to stay in Chicago, though they eventually traded him.) Though he doesn’t quite have the clean health record and complete resume to reset the market, a two-time Pro Bowler and 2024 Second Team All-Pro won’t come cheap. If Johnson is able to remain healthy and anchor a defensive secondary that will be instrumental in holding down this year’s your-guess-is-as-good-as-mine defense, the Bears are going to have some intriguing discussions ahead for them. Because not only is Johnson capable of locking up some of the best receivers in football when he’s operating at full capacity, but he’s also the only sure thing Chicago has at cornerback, with Kyler Gordon constantly battling soft tissue injuries, Tyrique Stevenson struggling with consistency, and rookie fourth-round Malik Mohammad needing experience. It makes sense to get something done with Johnson sooner rather than later, assuming health and everything else pass the vibe check, to avoid the price rising out of reach. More likely than not, Chicago will let things play out a bit longer with Johnson and see if his body will justify the investment. After all, the Bears also have some major money to shell out in the future to the likes of Caleb Williams and (eventually) Colston Loveland and want to be careful with their spending, which is already bumping up against the cap. But seeing as how the Bears are placed, it might behoove them to watch what the Seahawks do with Witherspoon and how the Patriots spend on Gonzalez and see if a slightly discounted version might not help them keep arguably their best defensive player around a while longer.
author: Khari Thompson

title: Bears QB Caleb Williams ranks No. 51 in NFL Top 100
summary: The NFL has been releasing its NFL Top 100 participants slowly over the last few weeks, and on Friday, the moment came that Bears fans were waiting for: Caleb Williams was announced as the No. 51 player on their list. This marks Williams’ first appearance on the annual list as he ends into his third […]
full_text: The NFL has been releasing its NFL Top 100 participants slowly over the last few weeks, and on Friday, the moment came that Bears fans were waiting for: Caleb Williams was announced as the No. 51 player on their list. This marks Williams’ first appearance on the annual list as he ends into his third season in the NFL. It also marks only the second time that a Bears quarterback has appeared on the list since its inception in 2011; Justin Fields was the first to appear with his No. 86 ranking in 2023. It’s been a strong offseason of hype for Williams, and much of it has been warranted. He’s coming off a year in which he led Chicago to their first NFC North crown since 2018, as well as their first playoff victory since 2011. He earned cover athlete recognition on the front of Madden NFL 27 , making him the first Bears player to ever receive cover athlete status on a standard edition of the game. It’s also worth mentioning he came in as the No. 90 entrant in Pro Football Network’s Top 100 list , as well. In 17 games last season, Williams threw for 3,942 yards, a single-season record in Bears history. He also threw for 27 touchdowns to just seven interceptions on a 58.1% completion percentage, adding 388 rushing yards and three rushing touchdowns to the mix.

title: Training Camp Battle: LT: Braxton Jones vs Jedrick Wills vs Theo Benedet
summary: The Chicago Bears’ offensive line has felt like a dumpster fire for years and years. After Ryan Pace’s offensive line fell apart the last couple of years, Ryan Poles took a long time to address the offensive line and didn’t do too much outside of Darnell Wright until Ben Johnson arrived. Finally, in 2025, Bears […]
full_text: LAKE FOREST, ILLINOIS - JUNE 10: Braxton Jones #70 of the Chicago Bears speaks to media after Chicago Bears Minicamp at Halas Hall on June 10, 2026 in Lake Forest, Illinois. (Photo by Geoff Stellfox/Getty Images) | Getty Images The Chicago Bears’ offensive line has felt like a dumpster fire for years and years. After Ryan Pace’s offensive line fell apart the last couple of years, Ryan Poles took a long time to address the offensive line and didn’t do too much outside of Darnell Wright until Ben Johnson arrived. Finally, in 2025, Bears fans got the offensive line they had been dreaming of. There was stability. There was talent. There was success. The Bears had one of the best offensive lines in the league. But then the playoffs hit, and Ozzy Trapilo was hit with a catastrophic knee injury, and two months later, Drew Dalman retired. Sometimes you wonder if Bears fans truly can’t have nice things. We’ve already talked about the training camp battle that will happen between Garrett Bradbury and Logan Jones with the departure of Drew Dalman. Now let’s talk about the left tackle position with the injury to Trapilo. Let’s start with Trapilo. We know the Bears are going to be without him to start the season. But there is no indication at this point as to when exactly he would return. Optimistic timetables would hope he returns in October and that this left tackle situation may only last for 6 or 7 games. More conservative timetables have him missing the entire season, or at least most of it. On top of that, we don’t know how effective Trapilo will be and how well that knee will hold up and bend when he’s out there. It’s possible that even if Trapilo is back, he isn’t quite ready to actually be back, and he may struggle. Without knowing exactly what Trapilo’s situation will be, it’s a safer bet to assume the conservative estimates are more accurate. If the more optimistic estimates come to fruition and Trapilo can play and play well, that’s icing on the cake and great news. But you’d rather be prepared for the worst and hope for the best. If Trapilo is out for most of the year, it puts the Bears in a tricky situation of needing to find a solid left tackle for one season so Trapilo can take his spot back in 2027. To do that, the Bears have three potential candidates to fill in for Trapilo. Theo Benedet, Braxton Jones, and Jedrick Wills. Let’s start with Benedet. Personally, I don’t think Benedet factors in here unless both Jones and Wills are disasters. Benedet was the break-glass in case of emergency last year after both Jones and Trapilo weren’t ready to play out of the gates, and I think he fills the same role this year. Benedet struggles to pass protection off the edge, and if we are being honest, we definitely saw the passing game come together more when Trapilo strengthened the pass protection. Also, keep in mind that after Trapilo was injured, Ben Johnson chose to bump Joe Thuney out to LT and play Jordan McFadden rather than have Benedet play in the playoffs. That’s telling. So let’s look at what presumably are the two main candidates here: Wills and Jones. Let’s start with Wills, who is a unique case. Wills was a top-ten pick back in 2020 and played decently for the Cleveland Browns. He was inconsistent in the run game, and there was a lot of talk about whether he loved football and had the competitive fire to do what was necessary in run blocking. His pass blocking was generally considered solid. Wills suffered multiple injuries that caused him to basically have realignment surgery to get his lower half right and sat out the 2025 season. Does Wills have the mental fortitude to fight all the way back and try to earn a starting position? The talent isn’t the problem. If Ben Johnson and Dan Roushar can show Wills what it takes to be successful at this level and pull the talent out of him, this could be a steal of a signing. If Wills shows that he’s not that interested in fighting for a starting position and a spot on the Bears, he simply isn’t going to be here in September. That leaves Braxton Jones, who is just kind of the default choice. Jones had been one of Ryan Poles’ best draft picks through the first three seasons of his career. Finding a starting left tackle in round 5 is nearly impossible to do, but credit Poles for doing it. Jones was solid, but injured his ankle at the end of the 2024 season and was never able to put it together in 2025. Was the injury too much to overcome? Was he simply not strong enough? Was he struggling in the scheme? Was it all of the above? Jones certainly has questions, and the rest of the league believes that too, as he didn’t have offers beating down his door. If Jones gets back to the player he was from 2022 to 2024, the Bears will have themselves a perfectly capable left tackle who can go out and get paid in 2027 after a nice 2026. If Jones looks like the guy from 2025, that’s not a guy Ben Johnson is going to have interest in starting on his offensive line. Perhaps that opens the door for Wills. Perhaps they go back to Benedet. Perhaps they go wild and sign Taylor Decker. Anything is possible if Jones doesn’t return to the player he was previously. This left tackle battle is critically important for Caleb Williams and the offense. They need competency opposite Darnell Wright. They can’t have a revolving door over there that’s constantly allowing pressure and forcing Caleb Williams to play backyard football all game long. If Jones can prove he’s back, the job will be his, but if he opens the door, anything is possible. I think Jones will be good enough to earn the job. I think he will be better than he was in 2025, but I don’t think he will be as good as the player we saw from 2022 to 2024. If that’s the case, the Bears will certainly hope that the more optimistic outlooks for Trapilo become fact and not fiction.

title: Chicago Bears 2026 Training Camp Position Breakdown: Cornerback
summary: Last season, the Chicago Bears had three cornerbacks spend all of, or most of, the year on injured reserve. Two of those players appear to be back and ready to go for training camp, Jaylon Johnson and Terell Smith, but the third, Kyler Gordon, has missed time this offseason with what was reported to be […]
full_text: Jan 10, 2026; Chicago, IL, USA; Chicago Bears cornerback Kyler Gordon (6) celebrates with a teammate following the game against the Green Bay Packers in an NFC Wild Card Round game at Soldier Field. Mandatory Credit: Matt Marton-Imagn Images | Matt Marton-Imagn Images Last season, the Chicago Bears had three cornerbacks spend all of, or most of, the year on injured reserve. Two of those players appear to be back and ready to go for training camp, Jaylon Johnson and Terell Smith, but the third, Kyler Gordon, has missed time this offseason with what was reported to be a soft tissue injury. Roster Locks There’s no question the Bears are better with Gordon on the field. His versatility opens things up for Dennis Allen, which is why he was paid so handsomely before the 2025 season. But missing so many games last year and now missing time during the offseason workouts must have head coach Ben Johnson a bit miffed. “This spring was going to be a springboard for us to get going in the right direction,” Johnson said last month via the Chicago Sun-Times . “So, you know, we’re still working through that. We’re still trying to get that availability piece going. We know he’s a good player when he’s out there, but trust level is a huge thing for this team, for this coaching staff, for the locker room, and you can only develop that trust by being available.” Gordon’s deal runs through the 2028 season, and contractually, the Bears would take a big dead cap hit if they moved on before that season, so they need him to get right and be one of the best nickels in the game for at least the next two years. Jaylon Johnson was slowed a bit during the offseason, but earlier this month, in a social media post, his foot specialist declared him to be 100% . Tyrique Stevenson is probably the odds-on favorite to start at corner opposite Jaylon, but he needs to be more consistent. The flashes have always been there — in 45 games over 3 years, he has 7 interceptions (1 TD), 38 passes defended, 5 forced fumbles, 2 fumble recoveries, and 3 tackles for loss — but it’s the lapses between the flashes that have been the issue, so hopefully that’s in the past. “The young man that reported last year is so totally different than the young man that’s reporting this year,” Stevenson’s position coach, Al Harris, recently said about him. “He’s focused in, he’s locked in.” Stevenson’s main competition could be fourth-round pick Malik Muhammad, but don’t be surprised if Muhammad is also working out at nickel. Josh Blackwell has been a core special teamer for Richard Hightower’s third phase since 2022. The Bears ended the 2025 season with eight cornerbacks on the 53-man roster, and they opened up week one with six of them. Cam Lewis, whom I mentioned with the safeties, has nickel experience and could factor into the depth of this position group. A Good Bet To Make It Since being a UDFA in 2022, Jaylon Jones has 6 starts across 56 games played for the Bears, and his ability to play outside, nickel, and special teams will likely find him back in Chicago. Terell Smith also shared a workout video earlier this month and looks to be good to go . He was drafted for the previous zone-based scheme, so we’ll need to see how he fits into Allen’s defense. I like his physicality, so if he can press, redirect, and recover, he should make the team. Roster Bubble/Practice Squad Dallis Flowers was on the Bears’ practice squad last year, and he was active for a game. In his 4-year career, he has appeared in 24 games with 5 starts. Dontae Manning was also on the Bears’ practice squad a year ago. Chicago has one UDFA corner on the roster this offseason, KC Eziomume from Tulane. His 4.38 forty at his pro day likely turned some heads. How many corners do you think they open the 2026 season with?

title: Bengals struggle in goal-to-go situations under Zac Taylor, despite their insanely talented offense
summary: The Cincinnati Bengals have the most talented offense in the NFL. With a top-tier quarterback in Joe Burrow and the league’s best wide receiver duo in Ja’Marr Chase and Tee Higgins, opposing defenses are often left to pick their poison and hope for the best. So why do they struggle so badly in goal-to-go situations? […]
full_text: INDIANAPOLIS, INDIANA - FEBRUARY 24: Head coach Zac Taylor of the Cincinnati Bengals speaks to the media during the 2026 NFL Scouting Combine at Lucas Oil Stadium on February 24, 2026 in Indianapolis, Indiana. (Photo by Justin Casterline/Getty Images) | Getty Images The Cincinnati Bengals have the most talented offense in the NFL. With a top-tier quarterback in Joe Burrow and the league’s best wide receiver duo in Ja’Marr Chase and Tee Higgins, opposing defenses are often left to pick their poison and hope for the best. So why do they struggle so badly in goal-to-go situations? An offense with this much talent shouldn’t have trouble punching the ball into the end zone after driving the length of the field. Yes, defenses become more condensed inside the 10-yard line, and there’s less space to operate, but that’s hardly enough to justify ranking 24th in the NFL in goal-to-go efficiency . And success in those situations matters. According to Warren Sharp , 74% of all rushing touchdowns are scored from inside the 10-yard line, while 55% of all touchdowns come in goal-to-go situations. The blame doesn’t fall on the players alone. Over the past five seasons, Burrow has been the third-most accurate passer in goal-to-go situations, yet the Bengals rank just 26th in EPA per play (-0.06) and 17th in success rate (44%). With a quarterback that accurate and receivers capable of winning quickly, Cincinnati should be able to spread defenses out and create favorable running lanes near the goal line. Instead, the offense has consistently underperformed in that area. If the Bengals are serious about making a Super Bowl run, that has to change. You can’t settle for chip-shot field goals in the postseason and expect to beat the NFL’s best teams. Cincinnati spent the offseason improving the roster and positioning itself for a deep playoff run. But none of those moves will matter as much if the offense continues leaving points on the field. Whether the defense takes a step forward or not, the Bengals need to turn more of those goal-to-go opportunities into touchdowns. If they’re forced into another season of winning shootouts, the difference between three points and seven could ultimately define how far this team goes.

title: Where does the “Who Dey!” chant rank among the best NFL team chants?
summary: The “Who Dey!” chant at Bengals games is one of the best parts of being a Bengals fan and a Cincinnati sports fan. When the Ruler of the Jungle leads The Jungle in the Who Dey chant before kickoff, that gets you going as a fan. After a big touchdown, that’s when the “Who Dey!” […]
full_text: A young Cincinnati Bengals fan cheers for the team in the second quarter of a NFL game between the Cincinnati Bengals and Arizona Cardinals, Sunday, Dec. 28, 2025, at Paycor Stadium in downtown Cincinnati. | Frank Bowen IV/The Enquirer / USA TODAY NETWORK via Imagn Images The “Who Dey!” chant at Bengals games is one of the best parts of being a Bengals fan and a Cincinnati sports fan. When the Ruler of the Jungle leads The Jungle in the Who Dey chant before kickoff, that gets you going as a fan. After a big touchdown, that’s when the “Who Dey!” chant is at its best. So, where does the chant rank among NFL stadium chants? Sports Illustrated’s Karl Rasmussen ranked the 10 best in the NFL, with the “Who Dey!” chant checking in at No. 6. If you’ve ever wondered how the “Who Dey!” chant came to be, here’s how, according to Rasmussen: The Bengals’ chant originated in 1981, stemming from a popular local car commercial and a beloved beer, Hudepohl. Beer vendors at the team’s former stomping grounds, Riverfront Stadium, used to offer the local beer by shouting “Hudy!” to fans. That eventually transitioned to “Who Dey,” and it evolved further after fans incorporated the song played in commercials by Red Frazier’s Ford of Cincinnati, which goes, “Who’s going to give you a better deal than Red Frazier … nobody!” The combination of both resulted in the Bengals chant. “Who dey? Who dey? Who dey say is gonna beat the Bengals? … Nobody!” Rasmussen also analyzes the comparison between the “Who Dey!” chant in Cincinnati and the “Who Dat!” chant in New Orleans that Saints fans do in the Superdome. In fact, he ranked the “Who Dat!” chant No. 5, one spot above the Bengals. Of course, there’s an ongoing debate between the two teams of which chant came first. One of my favorite memories as a Bengals fan was being at the Bengals-Saints game in New Orleans four years ago. There were so many Bengals fans who made the trip for the game. Before kickoff, Saints fans started doing the “Who Dat!” chant. In response, Bengals fans started doing the “Who Dey!” chant. It was dueling chants, making for an awesome pregame environment. Hopefully there will be many “Who Dey!” chants coming in 2026 at Paycor Stadium, especially against the Saints in Week 12 on Nov. 29, and on the road as well.

title: Joe Flacco earns spot on the 2026 NFL All-Backup Team
summary: The Cincinnati Bengals surprised us all when they traded for Joe Flacco in the middle of the season after Joe Burrow went down last year. The Bengals were crumbling quickly early on last season, but Flacco brought a spark the team, the fanbase, and city desperately needed. Despite a lack of wins, Flacco was incredibly […]
full_text: Cincinnati Bengals quarterback Joe Flacco (16) drops back to throw in the second quarter of the NFL Week 11 game between the Pittsburgh Steelers and the Cincinnati Bengals at Acrisure Stadium in Pittsburgh on Sunday, Nov. 16, 2025. The Steelers led 10-6 at halftime. | Sam Greene/The Enquirer / USA TODAY NETWORK via Imagn Images The Cincinnati Bengals surprised us all when they traded for Joe Flacco in the middle of the season after Joe Burrow went down last year. The Bengals were crumbling quickly early on last season, but Flacco brought a spark the team, the fanbase, and city desperately needed. Despite a lack of wins, Flacco was incredibly productive in Zac Taylor’s offense thanks to the help of Ja’Marr Chase and is now officially backing up Joe Burrow going into 2026. Bill Barnwell of ESPN recently shared his NFL All-Backup team going into the new season, and Flacco made the roster. “Here’s the veteran in our quarterback room. Flacco, 41, has been effective while bouncing around the league over the past three years, posting a 45.5 QBR while winning games for the Browns, Colts and Bengals. He’s going to throw some truly painful interceptions, but Flacco still has a strong arm, does a solid job of avoiding sacks and can run the offense from under center. He’s a great short-term option for us,” Barnwell wrote. Flacco is the most experienced QB that has been behind Burrow since he was drafted in 2020 and has now shown that he can win in the NFL and win with the offense in Cincinnati, if needed. As hard as it is to say, it is now important to have someone like Flacco behind Burrow after he went down with his third significant injury as a Bengal last year.

Cincy was historically bad against tight ends last year and has been a bottom-eight total defense three years running. The Bengals need to fix this issue — and fast — to seriously contend in the AFC. With Bryan Cook back there to solidify the back end of the defense with him, I think Battle will have even more freedom to get up near the line of scrimmage and make impact plays for this defense. Battle is also just 25 years old and should now be entering the prime of his career. title: Bengals founder Paul Brown ranked among the best NFL head coaches of all time
summary: Since the Cincinnati Bengals were founded in 1967, there have been a handful of names that are etched in football history, and one of those is Paul Brown. Brown founded the Bengals after his time with the Cleveland Browns and made a significant impact on NFL history during his time in Cincinnati. CBS Sports recently posted an article […]
full_text: Since the Cincinnati Bengals were founded in 1967, there have been a handful of names that are etched in football history, and one of those is Paul Brown. Brown founded the Bengals after his time with the Cleveland Browns and made a significant impact on NFL history during his time in Cincinnati. CBS Sports recently posted an article ranking the top-20 coaches in NFL history, and Brown is not only on the list, but he’s all the way up at No. 4, ahead of names like Don Shula and Chuck Noll. Only Bill Walsh, Vince Lombardi, and Bill Belichick are ranked higher. Here is some of what Bryan DeArdo wrote about Brown: After legendary runs at the high school level and at Ohio State (he led the Buckeyes to their first national title in 1942), Brown delivered an iconic run with the Browns that included seven championships over a 10-year span. Brown had a prolific partnership with quarterback Otto Graham, who led the Browns to a championship game appearance in each of his 10 seasons in Cleveland. Founded in 1946, the Browns won four straight championships in the All-American Football Conference before joining the NFL in 1950. The jump to the NFL didn’t slow down Brown’s team, as Cleveland captured NFL titles in 1950, 1954 and 1955. The Browns played for the championship in 1951, 1952 and 1953. Arguably the most innovative coach in NFL history, Brown is credited with creating practice squads, the draw play and the modern facemask. The first coach to hire a staff of full-time assistants, Brown is also the first coach to use game film to scout the opposition. Brown is also credited with helping break pro football’s color barrier. Brown’s personality (specifically, his hands-on approach, which included not allowing his quarterbacks to audible at the line of scrimmage) didn’t mesh with everyone, especially Art Modell, who relieved Brown of his duties less than two years after taking ownership of the Browns. Brown is not only a member of the Bengals Ring of Honor but also holds a spot in the NFL Hall of Fame. It is always incredibly neat to see such a prominent figure in the NFL world attached to the Bengals.
author: Patrick Carey

title: Bengals News: Boye Mafe breakout
summary: Part of the defensive rebuild this offseason was clearly to drastically improve the defensive line that struggled to create any pass rush last season. While most fans will look at Dexter Lawrence as the key to that (rightfully so), we can’t overlook the possibility of what Boye Mafe can bring to the table. Moe Moton […]
full_text: Bengals defensive end Boye Mafe speaks to the media during a press conference at Paycor Stadium in Cincinnati on Thursday, March 12, 2026. | Albert Cesare/The Enquirer / USA TODAY NETWORK via Imagn Images Part of the defensive rebuild this offseason was clearly to drastically improve the defensive line that struggled to create any pass rush last season. While most fans will look at Dexter Lawrence as the key to that (rightfully so), we can’t overlook the possibility of what Boye Mafe can bring to the table. Moe Moton from Bleacher Report is predicting Mafe to have a breakout year, and it makes tons of sense. Mafe was a rotational player with the Seattle Seahawks. It wasn’t really about him not being able to play a bigger role. Their defensive line was just incredibly deep, and the team wanted to rotate in fresh bodies as much as possible. Mafe was incredibly productive when he did get a chance—constantly being able to at least pressure the quarterback. Now he gets to play on a defensive line where it will be hard for offenses to get help blocking him on the outside with a presence like Lawrence in the middle demanding double teams. It wouldn’t be surprising at all to see Mafe have a very solid 2026 season where he rises into double-digit sacks. 7 Edge-Rushers on the Verge of a Breakout 2026 NFL Season After a few years in Pete Carroll’s and Mike Macdonald’s defenses, Mafe can be a versatile defender within the Bengals’ front seven. That said, expect play-caller Al Golden to unleash him in the pass rush. Elizabeth Blackburn: Lean In. Show Out. This Is Our Jungle. The organization made significant investments in the football team and our stadium. On the verge of a new season, the next wave are key investments in our effort, time and dedication. Our players and coaches put in the work every single week. They prepare. They compete. They push forward. Our fans are very invested — we collectively want to keep raising the bar and ask that, together, we lean in even more to continue building something meaningful. Bengals Snubbed in Latest List of Teams That Could Win the Super Bowl The Bengals definitely deserve to be on this list. Any team with a Joe Burrow-level quarterback has a shot at winning the Super Bowl. They are a dark horse team, not one of the first teams people will list. However, to keep them off is just not paying attention to what they do. Deebo Samuel, free-agent WR, could land with Bengals, per CBS Sports “This landing spot was recommended by CBS Sports’ Mike Renner,” Jordan Dajani wrote. “Some would claim the Cincinnati Bengals have one of the best wide receiving corps in the NFL with Ja’Marr Chase and Tee Higgins, but apart from those two pass-catchers, it’s questionable. Andrei Iosivas is the No. 3, followed by players like Mitchell Tinsley, Charlie Jones and the rookie Colbie Young. Imagine Joe Burrow operating out of 11 personnel with Chase, Higgins and then Samuel running around in the slot.” Former Bengals RB Joe Mixon reportedly done with NFL A pretty unfortunate ending to a good career. Mixon was a huge part of turning around the culture for Cincinnati when Zac Taylor came in. He was also very productive despite the terrible offensive lines he played behind for most of his career.

title: Dan Pitcher may not be in Cincinnati after the 2026 season: Why that’s a good thing

full_text: Oct 8, 2023; Glendale, Arizona, USA; Cincinnati Bengals offensive coordinator Dan Pitcher against the Arizona Cardinals at State Farm Stadium. Mandatory Credit: Mark J. Rebilas-USA TODAY Sports If you want to use a measurement of success for the Bengals in 2026, consider one that doesn’t pertain to wins and losses and how far they go in the playoffs. In addition to that, consider it from offensive coordinator Dan Pitcher’s perspective. Pitcher is an up-and-coming head coaching candidate in the NFL. That means he may be a head coach as early as next year. If you’re a Bengals’ fan, yes, that would mean he wouldn’t be the Bengals’ offensive coordinator in 2027. However, if Pitcher is going to be an attractive head coaching candidate come mid-January, that’s a good thing. That probably means the Bengals’ offense would have been very good in the regular season. Jourdan Rodrigue, who is a tremendous national NFL writer for The Athletic and a regular guest on the NFL Daily podcast with Gregg Rosenthal, recently named a breakout candidate on the coaching staffs of the 32 teams in the NFL . For the Bengals, she mentioned Dan Pitcher. “Pitcher has drawn interest from other teams for both head coach and offensive coordinator positions,” Rodrigue wrote. “With Cincinnati clearly swinging for the fences after an active offseason in hopes of maximizing quarterback Joe Burrow’s prime, Pitcher could receive an even larger spotlight. Senior writer Paul Dehner Jr. also mentioned tight ends coach and run game coordinator James Casey, who he says is ‘beloved’ in the building and has a big role in setting up the run-pass marriage for the rest of the offense.” Here’s another thing that interests me. If the Bengals’ offense is great this season, Pitcher isn’t going to just get interviews from teams that are desperate, a la Cleveland and Las Vegas. He’s going to attract interviews from teams that actually need head coaches and recognize what Pitcher has done with Joe Burrow and the Bengals’ offense. There’s a real chance Pitcher may not be on the Bengals’ coaching staff in 2027. That might not sit well with Bengals fans, but it would be a product of the Bengals being really good on offense this season, and that would probably result in a postseason berth. If Pitcher is also getting interviews for head coaching jobs while the Bengals are in a playoff run, that would be a good thing.

(Photo by David Jensen/Getty Images) | Getty Images While the Cleveland Browns have rookies and a few veterans having already reported to training camp , the full squad won’t be in action until early next week. Around the NFL, a few teams have already started training camp practice with media in attendance. The Arizona Cardinals and Carolina Panthers, who play in the Hall of Fame game this preseason, were the first to start camp on July 22nd. The Panthers show up on Cleveland’s schedule this year , in Week 3 as the Browns home opener for the 2026 season. As we saw when Cleveland placed DT Maliek Collins on the active/PUP list , injuries are always a story in the NFL. Carolina is already dealing with more than their fair share of issues on the medical front. In back-to-back days, before camp even started, the Panthers placed a number of would-be starters on different injury lists: CB Jaycee Horn – Non-Football Injury – Due to stitches in his foot OL Taylor Moton – Non-Football Injury – Due to blood clots OL Ikem Ekwonu – PUP – Torn patellar tendon recovery DT Tershawn Wharton – PUP – Neck surgery DT Bobby Brown III – Non-Football Injury – Hamstring According to our Panthers SB Nation site , Moton, Ekwonu, and Wharton’s seasons are up in the air and seem likely to be unavailable when they travel to face the Browns in Week 3. Horn and Brown are expected back on the field during the early part of training camp. Unfortunately for Carolina, the injury issues continued in their first training camp practice as DE/OLB Nic Scourton went down with a major injury , reportedly a torn ACL, and is likely out for the year. Scourton was the 51st overall pick in the 2025 NFL Draft and was expected to start across from free agent addition Jaelan Phillips as the team’s primary pass rushers. Last year, Scourton had five sacks, 47 tackles, seven tackles for loss, and nine QB hits as a rookie. Injuries are a part of the game, but Cleveland’s home opener opponent has been hit hard earlier in their 2026 training camp.

(Photo by Jason Miller/Getty Images) | Getty Images With everyone wondering about who will be the starting quarterback for the Cleveland Browns , the rest of the team’s roster has quickly become young and highly rated for that young talent . As always in the NFL, quarterback, head coach, owner, and offensive play caller tend to be the most important and widely discussed topics. Since Jimmy Haslam bought the Browns , the team has gone through its fair share of QBs and coaches. HC Todd Monken is next in line, while we await the winner of Deshaun Watson versus Shedeur Sanders . Last year, former first-round pick Kenny Pickett was one of many quarterbacks attempting to solve Cleveland’s longstanding issue. Acquired in a trade with the Philadelphia Eagles , Pickett seemed to have an early lead on the starter’s job before an injury all but eliminated him from contention. Interestingly, Pickett’s college coach, Pat Narduzzi, said that the quarterback was desperate to leave the Eagles ( as transcribed by Behind the Steel Curtain ): “The Eagles did not want to trade him,” Narduzzi said on 99.9 The Fan . “He begged to be traded because he wanted to compete, and he felt like he wasn’t going to have a chance to beat out Jalen Hurts.” With the Browns, Pickett did have a chance for the starting job before his injury, then was traded to the Las Vegas Raiders in exchange for a fifth-round pick . With the Raiders, Pickett played in six games, including two starts, completing 62% of his passes for 188 yards with one touchdown and two interceptions. This offseason, Pickett signed a one-year, $4 million contract to back up Bryce Young with the Carolina Panthers. Barring an injury, Pickett will once again not have a chance to start in 2026, which is what led him to “beg” for a trade in 2025. Join the conversation! summary: Quieter offseason has Cowboys focused on the right things – Todd Archer, ESPN This is exactly what the Cowboys needed. “There won’t be negotiations on a long-term deal,” Stephen Jones said. full_text: Quieter offseason has Cowboys focused on the right things – Todd Archer, ESPN This is exactly what the Cowboys needed. “There won’t be negotiations on a long-term deal,” Stephen Jones said. It was another perfect only with the Cowboys moment where contract negotiations have become a never-ending story. In 2023, All-Pro right guard Zack Martin held out of a portion of training camp looking to renegotiate his contract. In 2024, the talks surrounded the futures of Dak Prescott and CeeDee Lamb with the Pro Bowl wide receiver missing most of training camp before an extension was reached. Prescott’s record $60 million annual deal would be agreed to on the morning of the season opener. And then last year, the mess that surrounded Micah Parsons ‘ contract saga that eventually saw the All-Pro pass rusher traded to the Green Bay Packers a week before the 2025 season started. It all pointed to more drama in 2026. But Pickens, who will make $27.3 million on the tag, attended the mandatory minicamp in June and said he will not hold out of training camp. July 15, the deadline for Pickens to sign a long-term extension, came and went with barely a note . It was like a balloon that flitters away when the air is released. The potential of drama was gone. Dallas Cowboys Training Camp Primer: Five biggest storylines heading into Oxnard – Nick Harris, Fort Worth Star-Telegram Things to keep an eye on. New line of defense It’s a new year, and it’s a brand-new defense under new coordinator Christian Parker . And while there is quite a bit we can pull from his press availabilities about how much the unit will see change, it’s tough to truly envision it until it hits the field. How has he solved the communication problems that plagued the unit last season? How will the 3-4 scheme find consistent pressure? Who will hold the bulk of the responsibilities in the secondary? Those questions might not get full answers in Oxnard, but the on-field product that we will see will offer a ton of insight into the unit that Parker has constructed over the past six months. Personnel-wise, there are a lot of new faces with things to prove. Rashan Gary was traded from the only NFL team he’s known (Green Bay) in April. Jalen Thompson arrives with the biggest free agent contract in team history. Caleb Downs walks into the NFL with sky-high expectations , and fellow first-round pick Malachi Lawrence will be looked at for a premium role as well. After poor linebacker play in 2025, Dee Winters is back in DFW to see if he can be the solution in the middle . The expectations remain the same on offense. On defense, the level of play has to take a significant step forward. How far has it come? We’ll at least get a head start on answering that question in the next month. 2) Is Dak Prescott a legitimate MVP candidate for 2026? Patrik Walker, DallasCowboys.com Will Dak Prescott have himself in the MVP conversation this season? Patrik : It tickles me to see some people act as if this question is bold or unreasonable (I call that the “Cowboy Tax”) when, in actuality, it’s so reasonable that it almost earns a yawn from me. Let’s talk facts here, or science, if you will. Prescott is an All-Pro quarterback that has been at the front of the NFL MVP conversation not once or twice, but three times over the last five seasons — to the point where there’s a contingent that argues he should’ve won the honor over Lamar Jackson in 2023. So, can Prescott be a legitimate MVP candidate again when the 2026 season rolls around? Yes, and yes again. He’s at the top of his game. He’s got weapons galore. He’s got an offensive play-caller that invites fresh ideas and proved he can call a No. 1 offense. If the Cowboys’ defense plays up to expectation under Christian Parker, or at least above average, Prescott’s play won’t be wasted with a playoff-less campaign or early postseason exit and, then and only then, will the world be willing to give the former fourth-round pick his credit … following a playoff run that requires both sides of the team to show up every week and not just Prescott and the offense. (*yawns*) Former Cowboys QB Will Grier to join Dallas staff as assistant coach – Joseph Hoyt, Dallas Morning News Will Grier is back in Dallas. Former Dallas Cowboys and recently retired quarterback Will Grier will join the team as an offensive assistant coach, a person familiar with the move confirmed to The Dallas Morning News . Grier had briefly re-signed with the Carolina Panthers this offseason before ultimately deciding to retire earlier this month. The Cowboys actually had interest in adding Grier to the coaching staff this offseason before he signed with the Panthers. The offer, it appears, still stood. The 31-year-old spent the entirety of last season on the Cowboys practice squad , his second stint with the team. Tony Romo arrested on suspicion of intoxicated driving in Milwaukee – Saad Yousuf and Andrew Marchand, The Athletic The former Cowboys’ quarterback found touble. Lead NFL on CBS analyst and former Dallas Cowboys quarterback Tony Romo was arrested on suspicion of operating while intoxicated (OWI) Thursday evening, according to the Milwaukee County Sheriff’s Office. Romo was driving southbound on Interstate 43 in Milwaukee when he was pulled over. The arrest report obtained by The Athletic states that Romo performed poorly on the standardized field sobriety tests and was taken into custody as a result. Romo was released shortly after being booked and given a court date of Sept. 21. According to the Wisconsin Department of Transportation, a first-offense OWI carries a penalty of $150-$300, plus a $435 OWI surcharge. An OWI is Wisconsin’s equivalent to what other states call a DUI (driving under the influence) or DWI (driving while intoxicated). Daily discussion question: How will you spend the last weekend without Cowboys things going on?

summary: Ask anyone which Dallas Cowboys defensive rookie they are most excited to see throughout training camp and you will get the same answer over and over: Caleb Downs.
