title: Detroit Lions 2026 training camp preview: Adapting the LB room
summary: In this installment of our Detroit Lions 2026 training camp preview series, we continue to explore the defensive side of the ball by examining the Lions’ linebackers, speculating on current and future roles, and discussing how many players from this group could make the 53-man roster. Previous training camp previews: Roster construction Under the Brad […]
full_text: Detroit Lions linebacker Jack Campbell (46), left, and linebacker Derrick Barnes (55) practice during mini camp at Meijer Performance Center in Allen Park on Wednesday, June 17, 2026. | Junfu Han / USA TODAY NETWORK via Imagn Images In this installment of our Detroit Lions 2026 training camp preview series, we continue to explore the defensive side of the ball by examining the Lions’ linebackers, speculating on current and future roles, and discussing how many players from this group could make the 53-man roster. Previous training camp previews: Quarterback: Can Luke Altmyer force a QB3 role? Running back: How RB roles could shift in 2026 Wide receiver: WR depth roles up for grabs Tight end: How many TEs will make the roster? Offensive tackle: Can Blake Miller win the starting RT job? Interior OL: How quickly will Cade Mays adapt to scheme? Defensive tackles: DT has upgraded starters, questionable depth Edge rushers: 4 big questions at the EDGE Roster construction Under the Brad Holmes and Dan Campbell regime, the Lions have heavily leaned on their linebacker group to contribute on special teams, which is why they tend to keep a larger number of linebackers than other teams. Six has previously been the magic number when speculating roster decisions. Let’s take a look at what they’ve done at linebacker in the previous five seasons: 2021 : Opened the season with five linebackers, using three on defense and two on special teams. Another special teamer was added mid-season, and they ended the year with six. 2022 : The pattern of starting with five but ending with six was repeated. 2023 : The Lions started the season with six this time around and finished with six once again. 2024 : With the expansion of the SAM role, the Lions opened and closed the season with seven linebackers, while only keeping six active on most game days. 2025 : The Lions opened with seven linebackers (while Trevor Nowaske was injured) but reduced to six in Week 3, where they stayed for the remainder of the season. How a planned increase in nickel defense impacts the LB room While the Lions have insisted that their core defensive principles are not changing in 2026, they have acknowledged there will be some tweaks, including utilizing more nickel sets . The Lions used more base sets (three linebackers on the field) than any team in the NFL in 2025, but a shift in personnel this offseason indicates that the Lions are indeed being truthful in planning on more subpackage sets (two or one linebacker). Traditionally, the Lions have kept six linebackers on their roster, deploying three starters and keeping three primarily for special teams and specialized roles. As a result, the Lions enter training camp with 10-12 linebackers on their 90-man roster and allow them to compete for jobs; this season they’ll enter training camp with just eight. In addition to entering training camp with two-thirds of the linebackers they normally do, there was a significant personnel change this offseason as well, as the Lions will be adjusting to the loss of starter Alex Anzalone, who departed for the Buccaneers in free agency. Anzalone was a captain and key cog in the Lions’ defense for the last five seasons, but a contract dispute and a shift to youth on the roster for salary purposes resulted in a split. Lastly, the Lions elected not to re-sign core special teamer Grant Stuard, LB7 Zach Cunningham, and practice squader Ezekiel Turner. To account for the loss of Anzalone and others, the Lions re-signed Malcolm Rodriguez and Trevor Nowaske, signed veterans Damone Clark and Joe Bachie in free agency, then drafted Jimmy Rolder in the fourth round, and signed rookie UDFA Erick Hunter after the NFL Draft. How much the Lions lean into subpackage vs. base packages will directly impact how they divvy up roles and which players fit each new role best. The battleground How will the use of more subpackages impact the starters? Not only will a shift to more subpackage use mean fewer three-linebacker sets, but the basic roles of the starters will also adjust. All-Pro Jack Campbell is entering his third season as the Lions MIKE linebacker, and for the most part, his role will only be tweaked slightly. In three linebacker sets, he’ll mostly set up directly in the middle of the defense, and will only shift his spot a few feet (from over the center to over the guard) in nickel subpackage looks. Of course, with Campbell’s range he’ll work from all over the field, but as a general rule, he’ll be in the center of the defense. Derrick Barnes was the starting SAM linebacker last season, a role that asked him to line up outside the tackle box on most plays, giving him the option to defend the run, pursue from the backside, pass rush, or drop into coverage. In three linebacker sets, Barnes is expected to remain in this role. In subpackages, when only two linebackers are on the field, Barnes is expected to shift to a WILL (INSIDE) linebacker role, which is very different than the role Anzalone played last season. In three-linebacker sets, a traditional WILL lines up outside the tackle box, but in two-linebacker sets, the position shifts INSIDE, lining up over the tackle/guard gap, allowing the nickel defender room to operate. Here’s an example from Week 18 when Anzalone missed the game due to a concussion: While Barnes is expected to shift roles depending on base/subpackage sets, the Lions will still need a LB3 to play a traditional WILL role when they deploy three linebackers. Who is LB3 heading into training camp? While Campbell and Barnes are expected to fill the primary two linebacker roles, the Lions still plan on deploying three-linebacker sets, and heading into training camp, the leading candidate for that role is Malcolm Rodriguez. Rodriguez tore his ACL in 2024, and while he was able to return to action late last season, he still looked like he was re-acclimating to football. That being said, in Week 18 when Anzalone was unavailable, Rodriguez was elevated to an LB3 role and was on the field for 75% of defensive snaps. With an offseason/training camp to prepare and an opportunity to step into a LB3 role, expectations are high that he can rejoin the Lions’ starting lineup in base packages. However, he will face competition… What should Lions expect from rookie Jimmy Rolder? The developmental upside for Rolder is exciting , but expectations for his rookie season should be tempered. Learning the Lions’ linebacker roles can be incredibly challenging for a young player—remember, even Campbell didn’t start as a rookie—and Rolder enters the fray with only one year of college starting experience. Fortunately, he comes from a system at Michigan that runs a Pro-Style defensive scheme (molded after the Ravens), but even then, there’s a large jump in information and competition. Rolder should find the field immediately on special teams, could start the season as high as LB4 on the depth chart, and might even push Rodriguez for an LB3 role as he gains experience, but based on how the Lions typically bring their linebackers along, his impact on the defensive side of the ball may not come until 2027. Will the Lions reduce to 5 LBs, or stick with 6? After the top four linebackers, the Lions’ remaining four players will likely be battling it out for one or two remaining spots. Trevor Nowaske, based on his experience with the team, will likely enter training camp as LB4 and no lower than LB6. His skill set gives the Lions a backup to Barnes at the SAM, as well as depth at MIKE. Damone Clark could also fall into the LB4-6 range to start camp, and he should be in competition for WILL snaps and MIKE depth. Joe Bachie has six years of NFL experience, but he’s primarily been a special teamer. That being said, the Lions have kept special teams-only linebackers in the past, giving him a shot to stick. Rookie UDFA Erick Hunter rounds out the group, but his coverage skills could give him a chance to turn heads in training camp. It’s also worth…

title: 10 most polarizing Detroit Lions players of 2026
summary: On Thursday, we concluded our series ranking the Detroit Lions’ 2026 roster from 90 to 1. Our methodology was simple: eight people on the Pride of Detroit staff submitted their entire ballot, 90-1, and we averaged out the total votes to create a consensus list. You’ve had a chance to voice your opinion on our […]
full_text: Jun 17, 2026; Detroit, MI, USA; Detroit Lions running back Isiah Pacheco (10) runs the ball during the Detroit Lions veteran’s minicamp at the Allen Park Training Facility. Mandatory Credit: Lon Horwedel-Imagn Images | Lon Horwedel-Imagn Images On Thursday, we concluded our series ranking the Detroit Lions’ 2026 roster from 90 to 1 . Our methodology was simple: eight people on the Pride of Detroit staff submitted their entire ballot, 90-1, and we averaged out the total votes to create a consensus list. You’ve had a chance to voice your opinion on our list , and today, we’re going to pull the curtain back a little bit. Below are the 10 players who we had the biggest disagreements about. These are the players that had the widest range of rankings, and I’ll share each individual vote for each player, to see whether it was a couple of outlier votes or if we just couldn’t find a consensus. These players are ranked in reverse order from smallest disagreement to largest. The commentary is all my own. 10. LB Erick Hunter Final spot on rankings: 77 Highest ranking: 65 Lowest ranking: 88 Every vote: 65, 70, 71, 72, 74, 78, 82, 88 It’s not all that surprising to see an undrafted rookie make this list. The span of outcomes is rather large for that pool of players—especially for a small school player like Hunter (Morgan State). Still, there’s a lot of hope for Hunter among some fans and analysts. Given that there is also opportunity at linebacker, it’s understandable that a few staffers would put him on the roster bubble rather than a long shot. t-8. QB Teddy Bridgewater Final spot on rankings: 38 Highest ranking: 26 Lowest ranking: 50 Every vote: 26, 30, 34, 35, 38, 40, 44, 50 It’s certainly hard to gauge where Bridgewater is at in terms of his on-field skills considering he’s thrown just 15 passes in the last three seasons combined. Additionally, his value goes beyond his quarterback skills, as he’s a valued mentor to the Lions’ young quarterbacks and wide receivers. That intangible value may have vaulted his ranking by some, and some sketchy play for the Buccaneers last year may have dragged him down for others. t-8. EDGE Payton Turner Final spot on rankings: 51 Highest ranking: 39 Lowest ranking: 63 Every vote: 39, 45, 46, 47, 48, 51, 56, 63 Turner was a former first-round pick, and he fits the exact mold of what the Lions want opposite Aidan Hutchinson. But his first five seasons in the NFL have all been shortened by injuries. He played five games in 2021, eight in 2022, two in 2023, 16 in 2024, and zero in 2025. It’s understandable to be both extremely skeptical and at least mildly hopeful for Turner, hence the big disparity. 7. CB Avonte Maddox Final spot on rankings: 32 Highest ranking: 23 Lowest ranking: 48 Every vote: 23, 24, 28, 29, 37, 38, 46, 48 I’m fascinated by this range in votes, but I think it does represent how different expectations are for Maddox in 2026. On one hand, he could be a starting safety, starting nickel, or even a part of the outside cornerback depth room this season. On the other hand, the addition of Chuck Clark could potentially threaten Maddox’s spot on the roster entirely, as a veteran safety with more success and experience at the position. t-5. S Thomas Harper Final spot on rankings: 32 Highest ranking: 28 Lowest ranking: 54 Every vote: 28, 30, 31, 31, 33, 34, 40, 54 This is more the result of one outlier vote, as six of eight staffers had Harper ranked between 28-34, a very tight range by this rankings’ standards. Still, Harper has a lot to prove as a young player. He showed serious promise with the Raiders in 2024, and he fought valiantly as a reserve safety for Detroit last year. I don’t know if he can win a starting job in 2026, but it certainly seems like the Lions will keep him around to explore his full potential. t-5. S Chuck Clark Final spot on rankings: 41 Highest ranking: 26 Lowest ranking: 52 Every vote: 26, 33, 36, 39, 40, 44, 49, 52 Can you tell there is some serious disagreements and uncertainty around the safety position? I think Chuck Clark’s wide range can be easily explained by two quotes from Lions coaches this fall: Safeties coach Brian O’Neill: “There’s not a lot of what I call alpha communicators in the back seven. He’s one of them. He can run the whole show. He can run it all back there, so I’ve been really, really impressed with him.” Defensive coordinator Kelvin Sheppard: “When it comes to athletic ability, can he still do certain things? That is still yet to be seen, in training camp that it will allow us those four-to-five-week period to see what he is capable of doing.” Clark is a great mind, expert communicator, and will rarely make a mental mistake, but there are legitimate questions about whether he’s still physically got it at 31 years old. t-3. K Jake Bates Final spot on rankings: 31 Highest ranking: 24 Lowest ranking: 52 Every vote: 24, 24, 30, 32, 34, 37, 40, 52 This is another case of one outlier dragging the range wide. That said, some disagreement on Bates is warranted. For one, it’s simply hard to place a value on a special teamer as it relates to the rest of the team. Additionally, Bates has been a little inconsistent. After an outstanding first year in Detroit, making 89.7% of his field goals, that number dropped all the way to 79.4% last year. Still, the coaching staff has professed a lot of love for him, and he also improved his accuracy on the new kickoff format. t-3. LB Joe Bachie Final spot on rankings: 76 Highest ranking: 55 Lowest ranking: 83 Every vote: 55, 73, 75, 76, 77, 77, 79, 83 There is one clear outlier here, but it’s worth exploring because Bachie has not really been talked about much. He’s a six-year veteran linebacker who started five games last year for the Colts (before being waived with an injury designation) and has 1,128 snaps of experience on special teams. He probably has a better chance to make the Lions’ roster than most are giving him credit for, especially considering the lack of depth in that room. 2. RB Isiah Pacheco Final spot on rankings: 27 Highest ranking: 18 Lowest ranking: 48 Every vote: 18, 21, 23, 24, 25, 27, 29, 48 This is another case of one major outlier in the vote. And while everyone else has Pacheco as a top-30 player on this roster, it’s worth approaching his 2026 with some skepticism. Not only have injuries derailed Pacheco’s last two seasons with the Chiefs, but when he was on the field, it certainly looked like some of his explosiveness has been zapped. Now further removed from those injuries, will that return to his game? No one can say for sure. 1. P Jack Fox Final spot on rankings: 26 Highest ranking: 13 Lowest ranking: 51 Every vote: 13, 17, 23, 25, 26, 28, 30, 51 Ah, the punter dilemma. It’s a very hard position to place value upon, but I think the entire staff can agree Fox is one of the best punters in football. Should that land him a spot in the top 20? Or is that more something to celebrate in the 30s or 40s. The one 51 vote certainly dragged all of this down, and, no, it wasn’t me. In fact, you may be shocked to learn that I was the No. 13 vote. Not many on this team can brag about being a first-team All Pro player, and Fox is one of them.

title: Which Lions player or coach should be mic’d up for training camp?
summary: For as long as I have been a fan of the NFL, some of my favorite content outside of the actual games themselves has always been mic’d up segments. You get some of the most raw, hilarious, and sometimes iconic moments ever by having a player or coach mic’d up. In my opinion, that kind […]
full_text: For as long as I have been a fan of the NFL, some of my favorite content outside of the actual games themselves has always been mic’d up segments. You get some of the most raw, hilarious, and sometimes iconic moments ever by having a player or coach mic’d up. In my opinion, that kind of content will always be some of the most revered footage that NFL Films will ever have in their possession. With training camp kicking off next week, it got me thinking about times the Lions have opted to mic up a player or coach for a practice. As you probably already know if you are reading this, training camp in the NFL is a grind . Maybe not the grind it was back in the day, prior to the newer collective bargaining agreement getting rid of things like two-a-days and multiple padded practices in a single day. Still, even with the aforementioned limitations in place, it is a marathon of sorts. A long, winding road that seemingly takes forever to arrive at that first or second weekend of September. Going back to the Lions’ training camp in 2022, HBO’s “Hard Knocks” was in town, and the Lions, despite a lot of love for coach Dan Campbell and others, were still coming off of a 3-13-1 season. However, that didn’t deter coaches and players from having a good time in Allen Park. Remember the back-and-forth between former Lions coaches Duce Staley and Aaron Glenn? That brings us to today’s question of the day: who would you want the Lions to mic up for a training camp practice? My answer: I am going with Lions running backs coach Tashard Choice in hopes that we get something similar to the fun rivalry we had between Staley and Glenn several years ago. If you didn’t already know, Choice is good friends with Lions defensive coordinator Kelvin Sheppard. They are both Georgia natives, and played together during their time as players in the league. “Oh, I’m going to talk trash. We don’t like each other,” said Choice on his friendship with Sheppard. “I may fight him. It’s funny – when you’re in them (enemy) lines, I hate him as a player on the team, but I love him at the same time. You know what I mean? But you’ll see, that’s how we are. That’s the pushing part. Because we know when they’re going against him, they’re going to need that. My players are going to want to feed off of me. I’m going to feed off of them, and he’s the same way. So characteristics on how we are with our players are pretty similar.” What about you? Who would you want mic’d up for a training camp practice? Let us know in the comments below.

title: The Green Bay Packers announce an operating loss in 2025
summary: The Green Bay Packers are one of the few sports teams that have to “open their books” to the public due to the unique structure of the team’s ownership. Because the team is “publicly” owned, they have to announce what is happening financially with their club, down to reporting how much they made off of […]
full_text: GREEN BAY, WISCONSIN - DECEMBER 07: Micah Parsons #1 of the Green Bay Packers leaves the field after defeating the Chicago Bears 28-21 at Lambeau Field on December 07, 2025 in Green Bay, Wisconsin. (Photo by John Fisher/Getty Images) | Getty Images The Green Bay Packers are one of the few sports teams that have to “open their books” to the public due to the unique structure of the team’s ownership. Because the team is “publicly” owned, they have to announce what is happening financially with their club, down to reporting how much they made off of the league’s shared revenue streams — even if the NFL probably doesn’t like losing that piece of leverage against the NFL Players Association. According to Packers.com, the Packers had an operating loss of $1.1 million in 2025, in part due to a flurry of new contracts. Here’s how Green Bay explained its high operational costs: The Packers endured an uncommon year financially due to a combination of player acquisitions and departures. The structures of some new contracts, along with the required accounting of accelerated costs on released and traded players’ deals, all hit the ledger in the same year, which accounted for the $131.7 million increase in player costs. National revenue increased $20.6 million, or 4.8%, to a record $453.2 million, continuing the long-term growth and partnership the Packers have with the league. The 2025 home schedule included only eight regular-season games, down from nine in 2024. Local revenue, which encompasses ticketing, sponsorships, retail sales and events, still showed a productive $13.4 million increase despite one fewer home game. While the price of franchises has gone up nearly 10-fold in a decade, the league’s shared revenue went up “just” 4.8 percent last year, which is interesting. It puts into perspective how much money clubs are being infused with when ownerships around the league sell a piece of their pie, a growing trend now that private equity is allowed to buy up to 10 percent of teams, a rule that passed by owners by a 31-1 vote in 2024. It’s a good sign that local revenue has gone up with the Packers, even though they cannot count on playing nine home games every year moving forward. Even when the league eventually expands to an 18-game season, leadership in the NFL — including both commissioner Roger Goodell and NFL owners — has stated that the expectation is that each team will play one international game every year , meaning that the oscillation between 8 and 9 home games per year is likely to continue through the next Collective Bargaining Agreement. The Packers don’t seem too worried about their current situation, though, based on comments made by President and CEO Ed Policy: The bottom line: The operating numbers aren’t typical of those the Packers normally see, but they aren’t setting off any alarm bells within 1265 Lombardi Ave. “The NFL is more competitive and more expensive than ever,” Chairman of the Board, President and CEO Ed Policy said. “We want to ensure our football leadership has every tool in the toolbox to build a competitive roster, and we do.” … “The franchise remains in great shape,” Policy said. “In the short and medium term, there are no major financial concerns, and we will continue to do what it takes to compete as the NFL landscape changes and evolves, which includes being intentional on generating more local revenue. “We are however, keeping a very close eye on current trends and how they may impact our long-term financial health.” Those trends relate to the challenges the Packers may face in keeping up financially with the rest of the league’s clubs, which have access to capital via private equity and limited partners purchasing small, non-controlling stakes in teams. “It’s like other teams have an ATM that we don’t have,” Policy said, referring to private equity. Green Bay’s statement also mentioned the Lambeau Field situation, with the lease coming up in 2032: Other teams also have significant public money invested in their redeveloped or new stadiums, which allows them to spend more money on non-capped football operations. From the Packers’ perspective, Lambeau Field – which will soon be the league’s oldest stadium – will need considerable investment for continued maintenance, as well as future improvements to remain a cutting-edge facility. “It’s critical to have a long-term plan in conjunction with the city, county, state, and stadium district board to keep Lambeau Field both iconic and state-of-the-art,” said Policy. Expect to hear a lot about the Lambeau Field lease, especially if you live in the Green Bay area, as we inch closer to the 2032 deadline. Currently, the City of Green Bay actually owns Lambeau Field, not the Packers.

title: Rams to wear white-out uniforms vs. Packers on Thanksgiving Eve

title: Green Bay Packers News: Packers will look for answers on both lines in training camp
summary: We’re now just days away from the opening of the Green Bay Packers’ 2026 training camp. It has been a long offseason, but the pads will finally go on next week, with the team’s first practice set for next Wednesday, July 29. Over the following five weeks or so, the Packers will need to settle […]
full_text: EAST RUTHERFORD, NEW JERSEY - NOVEMBER 16: Jordan Morgan #77, Sean Rhyan #75, and Aaron Banks #65 of the Green Bay Packers huddle during an NFL football game against the New York Giants at MetLife Stadium on November 16, 2025 in East Rutherford, New Jersey. (Photo by Kevin Sabitus/Getty Images) | Getty Images We’re now just days away from the opening of the Green Bay Packers’ 2026 training camp. It has been a long offseason, but the pads will finally go on next week, with the team’s first practice set for next Wednesday, July 29 . Over the following five weeks or so, the Packers will need to settle on a roster, but also on the final roles across their offensive and defensive lines. Those two units both face significant questions this summer, but the questions are very different depending on which side of the football you’re on. Defensively, it’s all about determining a hierarchy on the edge and a plan for how to line up on the interior. With Micah Parsons likely to miss at least the first four games of the regular season for his ACL rehab, the need to assemble a passable pass rush is critical. Lukas Van Ness will lead that charge, but who will step up behind him? Rookie Dani Dennis-Sutton should have plenty of opportunities in camp to show that he deserves snaps early on as a rookie — and that his draft weekend slide to the 4th round was indeed a mistake by much of the NFL. The interior line’s questions instead focus around who will play what position — namely nose tackle when the team lines up with a 3-man front. On the offensive line, the questions are less about who plays where and more around whether the expected starters at several positions are ready for the big time. Only two spots on the line have the same likely starter as at the start of last season, with Aaron Banks at left guard and Zach Tom at right tackle. Otherwise, Jordan Morgan takes over at left tackle, Sean Rhyan has moved to center, and Anthony Belton likely gets the call at guard, rather than playing tackle as he did early last season. Can that unit gel in training camp, stay healthy, and become a consistent reliable unit? The Packers certainly hope they can answer in the affirmative over the course of the 2026 season. One Packers Rookie With Best Chance to Surprise Everyone (And Sack History) | SI.com If Dani Dennis-Sutton beats historical trends to become a sack machine in his rookie year despite being a day-three draft pick, it won’t surprise everyone — especially not most of us here at APC. Countdown to camp: Jordan Morgan takes over Packers’ blind side | Packers.com It’s about time. Frankly, after seeing how he played at tackle towards the end of the 2025 season, it’s a bit frustrating that he didn’t end up starting over Rasheed Walker last year. OL expert ranks Packers OL as 29th best in NFL entering 2026 | Packers Wire Given the Packers’ success in developing linemen over the years, it’s reasonable for fans to have a knee-jerk reaction to reject this analysis. Still, there are questions at multiple positions that need to be settled, with several players (including the aforementioned Morgan) lining up in different spots from where they played in much of 2025. LISTEN: 2026 Opponent Preview: Green Bay Packers | Bears Talk Underground Tex joins Larry Dyer for a quick look back at the Packers’ 2025 and a more lengthy preview of what to expect from Green Bay in the upcoming season. Ed Policy to preside over his first Packers shareholders meeting July 27 | Packersnews.com Who’s planning on going to the meeting on Monday? If you are, be ready for warm weather and a chance of scattered storms. Man tossed by Yellowstone bison says hitting the ground was the worst part | ABC News Well as the saying goes: it’s not the fall, it’s the landing.

title: A Decade of Chris Ballard: 2016 VS 2026 Colts DTs
summary: The Colts are about to finish the offseason with some post-draft free agency moves, marking the 10th offseason under Chris Ballard. The decade of Ballard’s management has been a wild rollercoaster ride, albeit not all of it due to Ballard himself. But after this Ballard decade, how does the Colts roster stack up from 2026 […]
full_text: INDIANAPOLIS, INDIANA - SEPTEMBER 14: Deforest Buckner #99 of the Indianapolis Colts tackles Bo Nix #10 of the Denver Broncos at Lucas Oil Stadium on September 14, 2025 in Indianapolis, Indiana. (Photo by Michael Hickey/Getty Images) | Getty Images The Colts are about to finish the offseason with some post-draft free agency moves, marking the 10th offseason under Chris Ballard. The decade of Ballard’s management has been a wild rollercoaster ride, albeit not all of it due to Ballard himself. But after this Ballard decade, how does the Colts roster stack up from 2026 compared to 2016, the last year of the Grigson era? In this position by position series, we breakdown each spot of the Colts roster to see if the Colts are better or worse than their counterparts from a decade ago. If you want to find our previous entries of this series, you can find them below: Quarterbacks Running Backs Wide Receivers Tight Ends Offensive Tackles Offensive Guards Centers Edge Rushers The series finishes up the trenches with DTs next! 2016 DTs: Kendall Langford, Zach Kerr, David Parry, Henry Anderson, Haason Ridgeway, TY McGill, Arthur Jones 2026 DTs: DeForest Buckner, Grover Stewart, Adetomiwa Adebawore, Colby Wooden, Jerry Tillery, Derrick Nnadi The 2016 DT room was not a position of strength, in part due to injury. Only Haasan Ridgeway and David Parry played all 16 games in the seasons with Langford missing 9 games, the late Arthur Jones missing 8 games, Henry Anderson missing 5 games, and TY McGill missing 11 games. All 7 DL each played 300+ snaps for the Colts in 2025. Former Ravens and Colts DE Arthur Jones has passed away at the age of 39. Baltimore drafted him in the 5th round of the 2011 NFL Draft and he went on to play 8 seasons in the league, spending time with the Ravens, Colts, and briefly Washington. Jones was a key piece of… pic.twitter.com/8CFKSyhhV5 — Preme Football (@premefootball) October 3, 2025 With the 2016 Colts running a 3-4 base scheme, this meant a lot of shuffling on the front for the trio of hand in the dirt linemen across various alignments. Overall the unit combined for: 71 Pressures (4.6% Pressure Rate) 22 QB Hits (1.4% Hit Rate) 10 Sacks (0.7% Sack Rate) 145 Tackles (89 Solo) 15 Tackles For Loss The 2026 unit is meanwhile going through a lot of changes, as Neville Gallimore, Eric Johnson II, and Chris Wormley are out as depth linemen but the Colts have added Colby Wooden (via the Zaire Franklin trade with the Green Bay Packers), and former Kansas City Chiefs Defensive Tackles Jerry Tillery and Derrick Nnadi. And to top it all off, this could be the last year of the dynamic duo of DeForest Buckner and Grover Stewart starting for the Colts since 2020. The two are entering their age 32 and 33 seasons respectively, and Buckner is coming off of a major neck injury. Clock is ticking on both of their times in the NFL and with the Colts, which could make 2026 the last chance to try to develop successors in house before one or both of them depart in Free Agency or retire. DeForest Buckner and Grover Stewart are pure COMEDY 🤣🤣🤣 pic.twitter.com/aeDOlKy1jz — JVL Football (@JVLFootball) June 9, 2025 Ultimately this group produced around the NFL in 2025: 117 Pressures (7.1% Pressure Rate) 22 QB Hits (1.3% Hit Rate) 10 Sacks (0.6% Sack Rate) 224 Tackles (111 Solo) 37 Tackles For Loss Of the Colts backups, there is plenty to note about the depth of this unit as the Colts prepare for post Buckner and Stewart life in the middle of their defense. Colby Wooden was used as a Nose Tackle in 2025 for the Packers, starting 16 games for them. Wooden is at 273 lbs, which is 1st percentile among all Defensive Tackles, let alone the typically massive space eating Nose Tackles. Despite what should’ve been a terrible spot for him size wise, Wooden led the Packers Defensive Linemen in Tackles, Solo Tackles, and was 3rd in Tackles for Loss behind only Micah Parsons and Rashan Gary. Expect him to slide back into 3 Technique behind DeForest Buckner and compete with Adetomiwa Adebawore for snaps in the rotation. #96 DT Colby Wooden Highlights. The Newest Indianapolis Colt. pic.twitter.com/jkMLXb9CGm https://t.co/zfgM0HWmsE — Football Performances (@NFLPerformances) March 7, 2026 Derrick Nnadi has started 98 games for the Kansas City Chiefs Defense over the past 8 years, predominantly with strong Defensive Coordinator Steve Spagnuolo at the helm. The former 3rd Round pick carved quite a career as a block eater for the Chiefs, helping free up their linebackers to make tackles, pushing the interior of the line to demand double teams, and helping free up pass rushers from getting chipped by Guards. Leo Chanel with the thump and tackle plus Derrick Nnadi quickly shedding his block. pic.twitter.com/IEUTIb3EmO — Nate Tice (@Nate_Tice) February 10, 2025 He was never the best player on the Chiefs Defense, but they kept him around for so long for a reason. He will now be the top backup Nose Tackle behind Grover Stewart. Adetomiwa Adebawore was admittedly a big draft crush of mine in 2023. Similar to the aforementioned Wooden, Adebawore was at times strangely miscast in college at Northwestern as a Nose Tackle despite being an undersized DT (5th percentile weight at 282 lbs for NFL DTs). Despite this role, he was fairly productive throughout his career at Northwestern, and developed in a strong pass rusher despite his raw technique and questionable role usage. Being one of the freakiest athletes in combine history certainly didn’t hurt, especially with his insane burst shown in agility drills, explosive testing, and his 10 yard split in the 40 yard dash showing his extremely quick get off on tape was no mirage. NFL+ has Adetomiwa Adebawore with a 17% pressure rate this season, which is just behind Laiatu Latu for best on the team His 2.73 seconds time to pressure is the 2nd fastest on the team, only trailing Tyquan Lewis. PFF has him as the 8th highest graded DT pass rusher in the NFL — Zach Hicks (@ZachHicks2) October 21, 2025 In 2025 Adebawore had a breakout, getting 4 sacks and 34 pressures in just 359 pass rush snaps. There was a stretch in the middle of the season where he was top 20 among DTs in win rate and pressures. The 25 year old still is growing and could be hitting a prime as a potential successor to Buckner as a pass rushing 3 Technique. Advantage: 2026 Colts Defensive Tackles Both units employ a deep rotation of Defensive Tackles, but the 2016 unit did so due to injury rather than depth. The 2026 unit has the better starters, with a healthy Buckner proving to be a top 10 and Pro Bowl level talent at his position for nearly a decade and Grover Stewart being long regarded as one of the better Nose Tackles/1 Techniques in the NFL. While there is a fascinating depth of both units, the 2026 unit has legitimate starting caliber players (Wooden and Nnadi) on good defenses now as backups on top of the best backup pass rushing DT of the two units in Adetomiwa Adebawore. title: Patrick Mahomes plans to do everything he did before for the Chiefs
summary: After Kansas City Chiefs head coach Andy Reid confirmed rumors that quarterback Patrick Mahomes will be a full participant to begin training camp, the MVP signal-caller talked through the latest checkpoint in his goal to start Week 1 “Monday Night Football” against the Denver Broncos at Arrowhead Stadium. The press conferences marked the official start […]
full_text: KANSAS CITY, MO - MAY 28: Quarterback Patrick Mahomes #15 of the Kansas City Chiefs follows through on a pass during the Kansas City Chiefs OTA's on May 28, 2026 at the Chiefs Training Facility in Kansas City, MO. (Photo by Scott Winters/Icon Sportswire via Getty Images) | Icon Sportswire via Getty Images After Kansas City Chiefs head coach Andy Reid confirmed rumors that quarterback Patrick Mahomes will be a full participant to begin training camp, the MVP signal-caller talked through the latest checkpoint in his goal to start Week 1 “Monday Night Football” against the Denver Broncos at Arrowhead Stadium. The press conferences marked the official start of camp, which could be one of the most challenging ever for Mahomes. Wearing the non-contact jersey that every quarterback wears in camp, it’s important to remember that “100%” in St. Joe doesn’t mean “100%” for a regular-season status. To that point, coach Reid doesn’t see camp being much different for Mahomes, expressing that when asked about it by reporters on Friday afternoon. “I don’t think it will be,” Reid answered. “We’ll see about the games and all that once we get there, but right now… he’s been given clearance.” “It was always the goal to be able to practice when we got to training camp,” Mahomes told reporters during his press conference. “So we’ve kind of hit that next step, and now, it’s just going to be about building.” After months of private rehabilitation, Chiefs Kingdom will now have eyes on their favorite quarterback for the rest of his journey to being ready to start in the season opener on September 14th. Mahomes sounds locked in on proving to all spectators that the injury and its recovery process won’t stop him from playing the position at its highest level. “You have to continue to work,” Mahomes said about himself. “Get better and better, and go throughout practice, prove to the coaches, prove to the doctors, everybody, that I’m the same quarterback I was before, if not better, and I can go out there, take care of myself and win football games.” "Prove to the coaches, prove to the doctors and everybody that I'm the same quarterback I was before, if not better." Patrick Mahomes shares his mindset coming back from a torn ACL and LCL ahead of training camp 👀 pic.twitter.com/964N8fWqXp — ESPN (@espn) July 24, 2026 “It’s a long process; the process isn’t over,” Mahomes acknowledged. “It’s something I’ll probably deal with for the next few years of my career and throughout the rest of my career. You have to stay on top of that stuff, but I feel comfortable now being able to go out there and run the offense the way it’s supposed to be run.” The Chiefs’ starting quarterback is ready for full-time practice, comfortable wearing a brace because he wore one in college. There’s no plan for when he could shed the additional protection. Regardless, Mahomes made it clear at one point in the press conference that he won’t be satisfied with any limited version of himself. “I plan to be able to do everything I did before,” Mahomes said. From here, he is focused on a list of things to improve on, just like any other year. “I’m obviously going to try and take care of myself a little bit better than I did last season,” Mahomes pointed out. “I think I ran a little bit too much last season, so I’ll try to be better with that.” The gunslinger was also reflective of his play before an injury came into the equation. “I feel like I wasn’t playing my best football at the end of last year before I got hurt,” Mahomes shared. “So I have to find ways to get better [at] navigating the pocket, running the offense better, getting the ball out of my hands and letting other guys make plays.” “I think this injury helped me kind of focus on those little things as I kind of get back to being who I am.” He believes he will need an emphasis on translating offseason gym strength to on-field quarterback play after spending most of his time in a weight room to rehabilitate. “When you talk to guys who have had the injury I had,” Mahomes began. “A lot of times, you feel stronger; I feel stronger than I’ve ever felt, as far as strength, lifting and stuff like that. So now, it’s just about getting that quarterback stuff down: moving in the pocket quick, making those quick movements, reacting and doing stuff like that.” Above all, Mahomes will need to make sure he’s available to the team for every game played by the Chiefs, all the way through the ultimate stage in February, potentially. As Patrick Mahomes builds to 100% from the knee injury, he remembers this play from his first game back from a knee dislocation in 2019 "It looks cool, but I actually did it because I was trying to get my knee out of there." Good example of 15 playing congizant of his knee pic.twitter.com/9z6notW6pc — Ron Kopp Jr (@RonOnChiefs) July 24, 2026 He will need to play with caution for his knee, something he has experience with from the 2019 season. Speaking with reporters, he remembered the first game returning from dislocating his knee that season: a loss to the Tennessee Titans . He made a highlight-reel throw that he revealed a key detail about: he made the jump throw in an attempt to keep his knee out of harm’s way in a muddied pocket. He admitted that it was a turning point in letting cautiousness from the injury affect his game. “After that play. I showed that I could be athletic,” Mahomes remembered. “I could jump off the knee I injured, and I can still make plays that I’ve always made.” We shouldn’t anticipate any jump passes in St. Joe, but Chiefs fans will be keeping an eye on Mahomes every day, watching him build back to feeling like the playmaker we’ve always known, and maybe more.
author: Ron Kopp Jr.

title: Andy Reid gives 6 Chiefs injury updates; Patrick Mahomes cleared to practice
summary: On Friday, the Kansas City Chiefs unofficially opened training camp as quarterbacks, rookies and select veterans arrived at Missouri Western State University in St. Joseph. Head coach Andy Reid began his opening remarks with a rundown of the team’s initial injury situation. At the start of camp, injured players can be played on the Active/Physically-Unable-to-Perform […]
full_text: KANSAS CITY, MISSOURI - JUNE 09: Patrick Mahomes #15 of the Kansas City Chiefs stands on the sidelines during mandatory minicamp at The University of Kansas Hospital Arrowhead Training Complex on June 09, 2026 in Kansas City, Missouri. (Photo by Aaron M. Sprecher/Getty Images) | Getty Images On Friday, the Kansas City Chiefs unofficially opened training camp as quarterbacks, rookies and select veterans arrived at Missouri Western State University in St. Joseph. Head coach Andy Reid began his opening remarks with a rundown of the team’s initial injury situation. At the start of camp, injured players can be played on the Active/Physically-Unable-to-Perform list (PUP). This gives players time to work back to health before being activated to practice. Players remaining on the list at the end of camp can be kept on the Reserve/PUP list to start the season — but they are then ruled out for the first four games of the season. Starting in Week 5, teams have five weeks to open a 21-day practice window to the return to the active roster before the players are moved to season-ending injured reserve. Once a player practices in training camp, he is no longer eligible for the PUP list. Per Reid, fans can definitely expect second-year defensive tackle Omarr Norman-Lott to be placed on the PUP list ahead of next week’s practices. Norman-Lott tore his ACL in Week 7 of the 2025 season. “Norman-Lott most likely will start on PUP,” Reid confirmed. “But he’s making progress. He had the ACL reconstruction, there.” Of course, Norman-Lott is far from the most famous Chiefs player coming back from a major knee injury. The eyes of the NFL are when star quarterback Patrick Mahomes can retake the field after tearing his ACL and LCL in December. Mahomes appears set to avoid the PUP list designation to start camp. Patrick Mahomes "has clearance to practice and do all the different periods of practice we have," Chiefs HC Andy Reid just said. Doctors will monitor ACL/LCL return. But "right now, he's been cleared to go ahead and participate fully." pic.twitter.com/2ux6hIQGoa — Jori Epstein (@JoriEpstein) July 24, 2026 “Pat’s doing great with his,” Reid declared. “Right now, he’s got clearance to practice and do all the different periods that we have in this camp. We’ll just take it day by day and see how he does. He’ll have plenty of eyes on him from coaches to trainers to doctors. But right now, he’s been cleared to go ahead and participate fully.” Late in the offseason, we learned that wide receiver Rashee Rice would be absent from the team both due to a short incarceration and a cleanup surgery on his previously injured knee. Reid also does not expect any limitations on the wideout’s participation. “Rashee Rice with his knee debridement,” Reid continued, “is doing great. He will go. We’ll keep an eye on him, but he’s cleared to go.” Rookie cornerback Mansoor Delane was sidelined at the Chiefs’ mandatory minicamp in June with what was later revealed to be a shoulder injury. Reid hopes that the sixth overall selection from April’s draft is on the verge of being cleared. “Delane is having his final physical, right now,” the coach revealed. “So, he’s right in the process of that but is doing well there.” Cornerback L’Jarius Sneed returns to the Chiefs after two seasons spent with the Tennessee Titans . In his previous tenure with the Chiefs, the team was very cautious with Sneed’s practice reps while managing multiple recurring injuries. Expect more of the same in Sneed’s second stint in Kansas City. “LJ Sneed,” remarked Reid, “We always kept an eye on him with his knee. We’ll just take him slowly and gradually get him back in the mix there was we go. We’re looking forward to getting him back on the field.” One deep roster player that Chiefs fans may not see any time soon is undrafted rookie tight end John Michael Gyllenborg, a Kansas City native and Rockhurst graduate. Gyllenborg was not seen on the field throughout the offseason program. Reid described the issue as a knee sprain. “Gyllenborg,” he stated, “he’s still working through the knee sprain he had. They’re doing some other evaluations on him. We’ll just see for this camp. Most likely, he won’t get much work.” If Gyllenborg is sidelined due to pre-exiting injury from college, he is likely heading to the team’s Acitve/Non-Football-Injury (NFI) list. Overall, Reid is pleased with the squad’s initial health. “Other than that,” he predicted, “I think everybody’s in a pretty good position to roll. Really, Norman-Lott’s the main one. Big guys with ACLs — it takes a little bit of time to get them back and fully strengthened up and ready to go.”
author: Jared Sapp

title: Chiefs training camp preview: Cornerbacks to watch on fringes of roster
summary: The Kansas City Chiefs cornerback room may not have many questions at the top of the depth chart, but the battle at the bottom could be one of the most competitive position fights in training camp. The Chiefs appear to have a strong foundation entering camp: first-round draft pick Mansoor Delane, Nohl Williams, Kristian Fulton, […]
full_text: Aug 9, 2025; Glendale, Arizona, USA; Kansas City Chiefs cornerback Melvin Smith Jr. (39) against the Arizona Cardinals during a preseason NFL game at State Farm Stadium. Mandatory Credit: Mark J. Rebilas-Imagn Images | Mark J. Rebilas-Imagn Images The Kansas City Chiefs cornerback room may not have many questions at the top of the depth chart, but the battle at the bottom could be one of the most competitive position fights in training camp. The Chiefs appear to have a strong foundation entering camp: first-round draft pick Mansoor Delane, Nohl Williams, Kristian Fulton, L’Jarius Sneed, Christian Roland-Wallace and rookie Jadon Canady all have inside tracks toward making the initial 53-man roster, leaving only a limited number of openings for the remaining cornerbacks. That reality creates an uphill climb for a handful of intriguing players, each hoping to force the coaching staff into a difficult decision. Here’s a look at the cornerbacks fighting to turn strong training camp performances into roster spots: Kaiir Elam: The former first-round pick No player in this group possesses a higher pedigree than Kaiir Elam. A first-round selection by the Buffalo Bills in 2022, Elam has already appeared in 43 NFL games while spending time with Buffalo, the Dallas Cowboys and the Tennessee Titans . While he has never fully lived up to his draft status, his physical tools remain evident. At 6 feet 1 inch tall, with nearly all of his NFL snaps coming as an outside cornerback, Elam brings legitimate NFL experience to Kansas City’s competition. Experience alone, however, won’t guarantee him a roster spot. The Chiefs have shown they’re willing to reward performance over draft pedigree, making Elam’s training camp critical. If he can recapture the confidence and consistency that made him a first-round talent, he could emerge as Kansas City’s final boundary corner. Melvin Smith Jr.: The developmental ‘sleeper’ Among the fringe players, Melvin Smith Jr. may quietly hold one of the strongest cases. After spending last season developing within the Chiefs organization, Smith enters camp with something none of the rookie hopefuls possess: familiarity with the system of defensive coordinator Steve Spagnuolo. The former Southern Arkansas standout also arrives with impressive athletic credentials, including a verified 40-yard dash time of 4.39 seconds and outstanding collegiate ball production, recording nine interceptions and 46 pass breakups during his college career. For players battling for the final roster spots, understanding the defensive terminology and expectations can often prove just as valuable as raw athleticism. Bryce Phillips: Built for special teams Every year, the final few roster spots are often won through special teams. That’s where undrafted rookie Bryce Phillips could make his strongest push. The former San Diego State cornerback played more than 700 defensive snaps in each of his final two collegiate seasons while earning a reputation as a physical defender who isn’t afraid to support the run. That mentality often translates well to units coordinated by Dave Toub. If Phillips consistently flashes as both a coverage defender and special teams contributor throughout August, he’ll give the coaching staff another difficult roster decision. D’Arco Perkins-McAllister: Length and versatility D’Arco Perkins-McAllister followed one of the more unique paths to Kansas City, playing at three different colleges before finishing at Louisiana-Monroe. That journey exposed him to multiple defensive systems while allowing him to develop positional versatility. Although primarily an outside corner, Perkins-McAllister also logged meaningful slot experience during his final collegiate season. Versatility has long been valued in Spagnuolo’s defense, but the rookie will likely need an exceptional preseason while proving he can contribute immediately on special teams. Zelmar Vedder: Betting on traits Sometimes NFL teams simply bet on physical upside. Zelmar Vedder fits that description. Standing 6 feet 3 inches tall, Vedder is the tallest cornerback among Kansas City’s developmental group. After transferring from Sacramento State to Houston for his final collegiate season, he demonstrated encouraging ball production while continuing to refine his game against higher-level competition. The size cannot be taught. The technique still can. Whether that development happens quickly enough to earn a roster spot remains one of training camp’s more intriguing storylines. The bottom line The numbers may ultimately dictate the competition more than the individual performances. Kansas City could keep five or six true cornerbacks depending on how it structures the rest of the secondary. If the projected locks remain healthy, that may leave just one opening for the entire group of bubble players. The Chiefs have historically adjusted the number of defensive backs the roster carries based on versatility and special teams value rather than simply keeping the most talented corners. That means every rep in St. Joe will matter. Elam brings NFL experience. Smith has a leg up with familiarity in the system. Phillips provides physicality. Perkins-McAllister has versatility. Vedder offers uncommon length and developmental upside. By the time the Chiefs trim the roster to 53 players, not all of these names will survive the cut. But if history has shown anything under general manager Brett Veach, it’s that one overlooked defensive back often emerges from training camp to become an unexpected contributor. At camp, look for the next success story to come from this list.
author: Maurice Elston

title: Around the AFC West: Preseason preview of our division foes
summary: Well, it’s that time of year again. NFL training camps are about to get underway, and every team in the AFC West has important questions to answer before the regular season begins. Here’s what to watch as the Denver Broncos, Las Vegas Raiders, and Los Angeles Chargers try to outdo the Kansas City Chiefs. Denver […]
full_text: KANSAS CITY, MO - DECEMBER 25: Bo Nix #10 of the Denver Broncos lines up before the snap during an NFL football game against the Kansas City Chiefs at GEHA Field at Arrowhead Stadium on December 25, 2025 in Kansas City, Missouri. (Photo by Cooper Neill/Getty Images) | Getty Images Well, it’s that time of year again. NFL training camps are about to get underway, and every team in the AFC West has important questions to answer before the regular season begins. Here’s what to watch as the Denver Broncos , Las Vegas Raiders , and Los Angeles Chargers try to outdo the Kansas City Chiefs . Denver Broncos The Broncos enter the season with one of the league’s most intriguing storylines: the health of quarterback Bo Nix. Nix suffered a significant ankle injury against the Buffalo Bills in the AFC Championship Game, and his recovery will be closely monitored throughout training camp. Despite the injury, Nix was ranked No. 59 in the “NFL Top 100 ”, showing the respect he has earned around the league after his breakout season. Another player to watch is wide receiver Pat Bryant. Before suffering a concussion last season, Bryant was emerging as one of Nix’s favorite targets. Out of wide receivers Troy Franklin and Marvin Mims Jr., Bryant’s ability to win contested catches should continue to earn him opportunities. Former Miami Dolphins receiver Jaylen Waddle’s presence could also create more favorable one-on-one matchups for Bryant. Broncos coach Sean Payton, from OTAs on the progress of WR Pat Bryant: "He's a quick study. He gets it real fast. I think one of his great skill sets is his run after the catch because his feet stay on the ground when he catches it. He's got strong hands in traffic. He's having a… pic.twitter.com/JShToH4q5s — Andrew Mason (@MaseDenver) July 18, 2026 The Broncos also have an interesting battle at running back. Can RJ Harvey seize the starting job? Veteran J.K. Dobbins re-signed on a one-year deal after leading Denver’s backfield last season, but injuries have been a recurring concern throughout his career. Following Dobbins’ injury, Harvey saw a much larger workload, recording 96 rushing attempts from Week 11 through the end of the season after totaling just 50 carries beforehand. Harvey also offers more versatility in the passing game, making him a reliable option on check-downs and wheel routes. If he continues to impress in camp, he could earn a larger share of the offense. Las Vegas Raiders The Raiders didn’t completely rebuild the offensive line, but the front office made significant upgrades by adding former Baltimore Ravens center Tyler Linderbaum and former San Francisco 49ers guard Spencer Burford, both of whom are expected to start this season. Las Vegas is also hoping left tackle Kolton Miller returns to full health after missing much of last season with a high ankle sprain and hairline fracture suffered in Week 4. Former second-round pick Jackson Powers-Johnson faces an important season, as does tackle D.J. Glaze. Both players will need to take a step forward if they hope to secure long-term roles with the organization. Perhaps the biggest storyline is rookie quarterback Fernando Mendoza, the No. 1 overall pick in the 2026 NFL Draft. Despite his draft status, Mendoza is not expected to open the season as the starter after the Raiders signed veteran Kirk Cousins during the offseason. Still, Mendoza has already generated buzz during rookie minicamp. Training camp will provide the first real glimpse at how quickly he can adjust to the NFL and whether he can begin pushing for playing time. Defensively, all eyes remain on edge rusher Maxx Crosby. After an offseason filled with trade speculation involving the Ravens before ultimately remaining in Las Vegas, Crosby appears motivated to prove he’s still one of the NFL’s premier pass rushers. Expect him to arrive at training camp with plenty to prove. First day out 😤 #RaiderNation pic.twitter.com/XcxWbFw8Ff — Las Vegas Raiders (@Raiders) July 23, 2026 Los Angeles Chargers For the Chargers, the biggest question remains the same as it seems to be every year: Can the offensive line stay healthy? Injuries have consistently plagued Los Angeles, including Rashawn Slater’s season-ending patellar tear last year. If Slater returns healthy alongside rookie Jake Slaughter, Tyler Biadasz, Cole Strange, and Joe Alt, the Chargers could field one of the NFL’s best offensive lines. The talent is there; the challenge is staying on the field. Another intriguing storyline is the team’s new tight end duo of Oronde Gadsden and David Njoku. Both players have shown they can take over games when given opportunities. Njoku never consistently found that opportunity with the Cleveland Browns , but he could thrive in Los Angeles. Head coach Jim Harbaugh has long favored using 12 personnel (two tight ends, one running back), and Justin Herbert has excelled in play-action concepts throughout his career. That combination could allow Njoku and Gadsden to become major contributors in the Chargers’ offense. Defensively, keep an eye on rookie edge rusher Akheem Mesidor. Currently behind future Hall of Famer Khalil Mack and Tuli Tuipulotu on the depth chart, Mesidor has an ideal opportunity to learn from two accomplished veterans. Chargers rookie Akheem Mesidor pic.twitter.com/GBVmqUnCGj — Kris Rhim (@krisrhim1) June 17, 2026 Mesidor enjoyed a productive final season at Miami alongside first-round pick Rueben Bain Jr., and if he continues to develop during training camp, he could carve out a meaningful role as a rookie rotational pass rusher. How do you think the division race can shake out this season? Do you see the Chiefs topping these three teams in the AFC West, or do the Broncos repeat? Can the Chargers finally win it? Let us know in the comments.
author: Kramer Sansone

title: The Chiefs are facing real doubt from football media ahead of 2026
summary: As a tried-and-true fan of the Kansas City Chiefs, there’s an unenjoyable thought that pops into my head, one that’s hard to shake. Maybe it’s happened for you recently, too. The question is simple: Is this how New England Patriots fans felt all those years? The past few years are really the first time I’ve […]
full_text: KANSAS CITY, MISSOURI - DECEMBER 14: Patrick Mahomes #15 of the Kansas City Chiefs warms up prior to the NFL football game against the Los Angeles Chargers at GEHA Field at Arrowhead Stadium on December 14, 2025 in Kansas City, Missouri. (Photo by Kevin Sabitus/Getty Images) | Getty Images As a tried-and-true fan of the Kansas City Chiefs , there’s an unenjoyable thought that pops into my head, one that’s hard to shake. Maybe it’s happened for you recently, too. The question is simple: Is this how New England Patriots fans felt all those years? The past few years are really the first time I’ve truly empathized with the loud, obnoxious Patriots fans from the era of head coach Bill Belichick and quarterback Tom Brady. It was boisterous, but why wouldn’t it be when winning is all a fan base knows for 20 years? Every doubt from fans and media alike seemed to spawn yet another chapter of New England’s dominance. It was remarkable and, from a Chiefs fan’s perspective, also incredibly annoying. Now, the roles have reversed. The Chiefs are now the dynasty everyone is trying to knock off. Picking Kansas City to win it all has become a boring choice. Everyone is searching for the next contender. And, to be fair, the Chiefs didn’t do much to quiet that narrative with a 6-11 performance last season. Add in an offseason that saw several key pieces depart, and some skepticism is only natural. What has surprised me is the level of it. People I consider thoughtful football minds, not exactly “hot take” artists, aren’t just doubting the Chiefs this year. They’re outright dismissing them. Connor Orr recently left Kansas City off his list of the 14 teams capable of winning the Super Bowl this year . That’s not a typo. He identified nearly half the league as legitimate title contenders, and the Chiefs were not among the group. Here’s the gist of his explanation: Th e league feels a bit more wide open than it did during the stretch when we could just pencil in the Chiefs to the AFC championship game and likely beyond… The Chiefs have, unquestionably, one of the two best quarterbacks in the NFL. They may very well win 11 or 12 games this season. But I don’t see how they can simply replace the losses of Jaylen Watson and Trent McDuffie while also running back essentially the same version of the offensive line for another year, especially if the team’s most significant offensive upgrade was at the running back position. .. The addition of Kenneth Walker III isn’t going to simply change the complexion of Kansas City’s offense, and even when Eric Bieniemy was previously the Chiefs’ OC, there was a failed attempt to create a more diverse, downhill running scheme to protect Patrick Mahomes. Orr isn’t alone. This has become one of the defining themes of the offseason. Another analyst I respect, Frank Schwab, recently ranked the Chiefs as just the 12th-best team in his NFL offseason power rankings . Putting the Chiefs at No. 12 is uncomfortable. .. But suddenly there are questions. There’s no bankable player in the Chiefs’ offense aside from Mahomes. KC’s defense has to be much better and is relying on rookies to fill key roles. Mahomes’ injury has become a non-story through the offseason but maybe it will be an ongoing issue. While it’s scary, we’re not picking the Chiefs to win the AFC West, though a return to the playoffs seems reasonable even if it won’t result in another Super Bowl trip. And that type of season wouldn’t get us much closer to an answer about whether the dynasty is still alive. The questions are legitimate. I have no idea how the wide receiver room is going to shake out. I’m not sure what the cornerback situation will ultimately look like. There are reasons for optimism, and if everyone stays healthy, I believe both position groups should be more than capable. But neither comes with any guarantees. The concerns about the defensive line aren’t going away, either. This team struggled to consistently pressure opposing quarterbacks last season, and the only notable upgrades to the front seven are a run-stuffing nose tackle and a pair of rookies. It might be enough. But skepticism is understandable. What I don’t understand, though, is why so many otherwise rational NFL analysts continue pointing to the offensive line as one of the Chiefs’ biggest weaknesses entering the season. It’s every bit as head-scratching now as it was during the draft season, when buzz started to pick up on the Chiefs spending a top-10 selection on an offensive tackle. Kansas City has arguably the best interior offensive line in the league. Josh Simmons showed above-average, and at times very good, left tackle play when healthy last year. The only real question is at right tackle, where the answer is very likely the $30 million player signed to the team a year ago in Jaylon Moore. Half of the league would gladly trade offensive line situations with the Chiefs heading into this season. All of it leads to a foreign reality for this portion of the Patrick Mahomes era. For the first time in years, the Chiefs feel like the hunters instead of the hunted. The Buffalo Bills , Denver Broncos and Patriots all seem to be entering the season with greater public expectations than the Chiefs. Some are picking the Chiefs to finish third in their own division . I’ve felt the doubt surrounding this team has been overstated in recent years. This year feels different. The skepticism is real, and it’s widespread. It’s becoming impossible to ignore. Maybe this really is how Patriots fans felt. Every offseason, outside voices declared the dynasty over. More often than not, Brady spent the upcoming season reminding everyone why it wasn’t. We’re about to find out if Mahomes can do the same for this era of Chiefs football.
author: Brandon Kiley

title: Chiefs with the highest career stakes this season: Justin Fields
summary: In this series, we will look at established players — virtual locks to make this year’s Kansas City Chiefs squad — with the most riding on the 2026 season. When the Chicago Bears selected Ohio State quarterback Justin Fields with the 11th selection of the 2021 NFL Draft, the player’s current situation was unlikely anywhere on his […]
full_text: KANSAS CITY, MISSOURI - JUNE 09: Justin Fields #6 of the Kansas City Chiefs throws a pass during mandatory minicamp at The University of Kansas Hospital Arrowhead Training Complex on June 09, 2026 in Kansas City, Missouri. (Photo by Aaron M. Sprecher/Getty Images) | Getty Images In this series, we will look at established players — virtual locks to make this year’s Kansas City Chiefs squad — with the most riding on the 2026 season. When the Chicago Bears selected Ohio State quarterback Justin Fields with the 11th selection of the 2021 NFL Draft, the player’s current situation was unlikely anywhere on his mind. Five years later, Fields finds himself the backup passer in Kansas City. After the Bears traded him to the Pittsburgh Steelers in 2024, the Chiefs will now be Fields’ third team in as many seasons. He spent 2025 with the New York Jets , who traded him to the Chiefs in March. At the time of Fields’ second trade, the Chiefs faced offseason questions with starting quarterback Patrick Mahomes early in the rehab process from a season-ending knee injury suffered in December. At his first three stops, Fields was auditioning to be a team’s regular quarterback, and he has been a Week 1 starter each of the last four seasons. It will be disappointing for Chiefs fans if that streak continues. With the Chiefs reportedly optimistic that Mahomes will be cleared before training camp begins next week, Fields will likely open the season on the bench. Ideally, Fields will not see the field at all this season other than finishing a game’s garbage time amidst a blowout Chiefs victory — or in package plays should head coach Andy Reid design special formations to take advantage of his rushing ability. Fields is scheduled to be a free agent after the season, and has already played for 12.5% of the NFL’s teams. If the Kansas City front office were to be entirely honest, the collective would probably prefer that rookie Garrett Nussmeier, the seventh-round pick from April’s draft, show enough over the season to take over as Mahomes’ backup in 2027. With the ever-increasing price of free agent backup quarterbacks, Nussmaier would offer a cost-controlled solution for at least three seasons. For his part, Fields undoubtedly still has aspirations to be a starter. This is a player who led Ohio State to the 2020 College Football National Championship Game and has started 53 NFL games. He may find himself a hard sell next spring at age 28 after already having three previous chances to claim a starting job. Fields’ biggest question in 2026 likely is whether or not he can transition seamlessly to a backup role. To be fair, a backup quarterback in the NFL can still be very lucrative employment. Former Missouri Tigers star Chase Daniel (the Chiefs’ backup quarterback from 2013-15) made a career $43 million over 13 seasons despite starting only 5 total games. Expected backups Jarrett Stidham of the Denver Broncos and Marcus Mariota of the Washington Commanders are each expected to make at least $7 million in 2026. Prospective future teams (including possibly the Chiefs) will want Fields to remain competitive while accepting his place in Kansas City’s quarterback room. The sixth-year pro could also benefit from showing a bit of versatility to his game (given the desirability of backup quarterbacks who can fit a variety of schemes). Fields’ running style will probably always offer more value than his arm, but he teased a higher ceiling as a passer in his short stint with the Steelers to start 2024. With Mahomes likely to be very limited in the Chiefs’ preseason slate, Fields should have plenty of exhibition opportunities with the Chiefs’ top players to show his ability to run Reid’s offense to audition for other teams (or for a longer stint in Kansas City). Ultimately, we will not know one of the biggest determining factors in Fields’ fit in a backup role: what he offers in the film room. The reputation he builds in game planning with a veteran (and well-connected) coaching staff will be very important in how teams see his career going forward. It will be an important year for where Fields’ career goes. With a deep quarterback class expected in next year’s draft, many teams will look for bridge starters for the 2027 season. If he underwhelms in preseason action or (in the worst-case scenario) in relief of Mahomes when the games matter, it could start to feel very late, very early on Fields’ career.
author: Jared Sapp

title: 52 Days until Chiefs football, we are ‘Creed Humphrey’ days away
summary: We are 52 days away from the Kansas City Chiefs‘ season-opening game against the Denver Broncos on “Monday Night Football” in Week 1. The No. 52 jersey is worn by center Creed Humphrey, who’s entering the season with two consecutive first-team All-Pro honors under his belt. He’s definitely the all-time No. 52 in franchise history, […]
full_text: KANSAS CITY, MISSOURI - SEPTEMBER 14: Creed Humphrey #52 of the Kansas City Chiefs runs onto the field prior to an NFL football game against the Philadelphia Eagles at GEHA Field at Arrowhead Stadium on September 14, 2025 in Kansas City, Missouri. (Photo by Kevin Sabitus/Getty Images) | Getty Images We are 52 days away from the Kansas City Chiefs ‘ season-opening game against the Denver Broncos on “Monday Night Football” in Week 1. The No. 52 jersey is worn by center Creed Humphrey, who’s entering the season with two consecutive first-team All-Pro honors under his belt. He’s definitely the all-time No. 52 in franchise history, but here are some others: The memorable No. 52s in franchise history Tom Howard (1977 – 1983) Bud Abell (1966 – 1968) Tracy Rogers (1990 – 1996) Howard played in a dark era of Chiefs football, but he was a full-time starting linebacker for seven seasons, racking up five interceptions, three forced fumbles, 17.5 sacks and two fumbles returned for a touchdown. He ended his NFL career with two seasons playing for the St. Louis Rams. 52.9%: Chiefs opponents red-zone touchdown percentage last season The Chiefs’ red-zone defense ranked eighth in the NFL in opposing touchdown rate (52.9%) while facing the 21st-ranked number of red-zone drives. It’s a reminder that the Chiefs’ defense held ground and kept the team in games constantly last season, allowing the offense a chance to answer. Whether the offense was able to or not was the difference between a close win and a close loss most of the time. The Chiefs’ defense needs to improve on third down, getting off the field and forcing more punts than field goals, but the foundation of a sound, above-average scoring defense is what defensive coordinator Steve Spagnuolo has built over his years at the helm of the unit.
author: Ron Kopp Jr.

title: Chiefs News: Mansoor Delane a player with something to prove in camp
summary: The latest Rookies for the Kansas City Chiefs will be reporting to the team’s training camp at Missouri Western State University in St. Joseph later today. When we are able to see the full squad next week, rookie cornerback Mansoor Delane will be among the players under the most scrutiny. Because of the price the […]
full_text: KANSAS CITY, MISSOURI - JUNE 09: Mansoor Delane #15 of the Kansas City Chiefs runs through a drill during mandatory minicamp at The University of Kansas Hospital Arrowhead Training Complex on June 09, 2026 in Kansas City, Missouri. (Photo by Aaron M. Sprecher/Getty Images) | Getty Images The latest Rookies for the Kansas City Chiefs will be reporting to the team’s training camp at Missouri Western State University in St. Joseph later today. When we are able to see the full squad next week, rookie cornerback Mansoor Delane will be among the players under the most scrutiny. Because of the price the Chiefs paid to move up three slots to sixth overall for Delane, there will be little patience for talk of a rookie curve. When assessing his camp, we will need to remember that cornerback mistakes are often magnified, and the position is rarely noticed when a player is performing well. That said, Delane needs to establish himself as one of the best in the league at his position quickly. Five Chiefs players with something to prove in training camp | The Athletic Mansoor Delane There are two truths when it comes to rookie cornerback Mansoor Delane: 1. Because the team traded up to select him with the No. 6 pick, he needs to be an immediate starter. 2. He didn’t get off to a smooth start in spring practices, sitting out mandatory minicamp with a shoulder injury. The second note might seem minor, but it could quickly turn into a big deal if Delane shows any ill effects when he arrives this week. The 1 UDFA with Best Chance to Make the Roster in Every NFL Team’s Training Camp | Bleacher Report Kansas City Chiefs: S Xavier Nwankpa In his pre-draft scouting report for Iowa safety Xavier Nwankpa, Bleacher Report’s Daniel Harms graded the 6’3″ 208-pounder as a fourth-round pick while touting his physicality against the run. “Nwankpa is routinely in the right place,” Harms said. “As such, he can wear a multitude of hats for a defense. He excels as a box safety, reading out plays and triggering downhill to make big hits…” As training camp opens, Chiefs point to brighter future in 2026 | ESPN KANSAS CITY, Mo. — Even a month ago, when the Kansas City Chiefs finished their mandatory minicamp, pass rusher Chris Jones acknowledged a reality that to him felt odd. “It’s been a while since I’ve had this long of a break with football,” Jones said, referencing the Chiefs missing the playoffs last season for the first time since 2014. Jones and the rest of the Chiefs have spent the past several weeks on another extended break, too, a hiatus that will be 42 days before training camp begins next week. When Jones rejoins his teammates on the practice fields on Missouri Western State’s campus, he and some of the Chiefs’ most prominent veterans have vowed to keep last season in their minds. NFL training camp: Top 5 unresolved issues | Yahoo Sports Will Patrick Mahomes look like his normal self? Mahomes tore his ACL and LCL late last season, but the stories about his recovery this offseason have all been positive. The team is hopeful Mahomes is cleared for training camp in the upcoming days, according to SI.com’s Albert Breer. But, like Daniel Jones, there’s a difference between being on the field and looking completely healthy. The Chiefs had a rough 2025 season and the only way they bounce back is if Mahomes is back to an MVP level. Jon Gruden and Ronde Barber will call Buccaneers-Chiefs preseason game | Pro Football Talk The Buccaneers announced that Gruden and Barber will be on the call for their August 22 home game against the Chiefs. Gruden has said he wants to be a play-by-play announcer, and now he will be, at least for one preseason game, for the franchise he coached to a Super Bowl XXXVII victory after the 2002 season. Barber was a Hall of Fame player on that team. Around the NFL Free-agent WR Tyreek Hill provides update after season-ending injury: ‘No power in my left leg’ | NFL.com “So it’s about 10 months after doing two surgeries,” Hill said. “My left leg is the one that I injured. I have no power in my left leg at all, so I’m trying to regain all the power back in my left leg. But it’s one day at a time.” The lack of a timetable for Hill to sign with a team falls in line with what his agent, Drew Rosenhaus, said last month. The goal is to get the speedster back into shape before he considers a landing spot. Ravens waive rookie Diego Pavia to make room for Ethan Pocic | ESPN After throwing 29 touchdown passes and rushing for 10 more, Pavia was named first-team All-American and SEC Offensive Player of the Year and won the Johnny Unitas Golden Arm Award as the best upperclassman quarterback in college football. Throughout the predraft process, there were questions about Pavia’s age (24), lack of height (5-foot-10) and decision-making off the field. After finishing runner-up to Heisman winner Fernando Mendoza in December, Pavia posted a photo on Instagram with the caption “F- ALL THE VOTERS” along with a thumbs-down emoji on social media. He later apologized. Sources: Panthers lose Nic Scourton to torn ACL on 1st day of camp | ESPN It’s a huge blow for the Panthers, who were counting on Scourton to be a top pass rusher opposite free agent addition Jaelan Phillips. Scourton went down on a wet field late in practice Thursday during team drills and players immediately gathered around him on one knee. He held his hand over his face as he was led into an awaiting cart. As he was leaving the field, the cart stopped and Canales and every player on the roster individually walked over to hug Scourton before he was taken to the training room. In case you missed it on Arrowhead Pride Can the Chiefs afford a ‘diet version’ of Patrick Mahomes in 2026? On Thursday morning, ESPN’s “Get Up” crew previewed the 2026 NFL season with a question about the Kansas City Chiefs : how good are the Chiefs if quarterback Patrick Mahomes can’t be 100% healthy this season? The question was first answered by former NFL wide receiver Andrew Hawkins, who doubted the team has enough “on the outside” to succeed like the organization has in past years of the Mahomes era, before pointing out that the quarterback may need to tweak his game to make it work.
