title: Commanders training camp: Antonio Williams among five rookies to watch
summary: Commanders rookies reported for training camp on Friday. Oh, and quarterbacks and some others coming off injury. All that’s standard, allowing the new folks a few days to get settled in before the full squad reports on Tuesday.   This pre-camp period came without much fanfare, though it’s an important stretch to help the rookies […]
full_text: Commanders rookies reported for training camp on Friday. Oh, and quarterbacks and some others coming off injury. All that’s standard, allowing the new folks a few days to get settled in before the full squad reports on Tuesday. This pre-camp period came without much fanfare, though it’s an important stretch to help the rookies hit the ground running next week while battling for roles and roster spots ahead of this 2026 campaign. It’s a seven-week stress test full of meetings, practices and walk-throughs where attention’s fully on football. Seeing how these players navigate their first camp will be revealing, though evaluation isn’t keyed to those avoiding mistakes. It’s about learning from them and maintaining the proper pace of absorbing information and then applying it. Washington needs several rookies to make an instant impact, while developing others for contributions over a longer term. There are several we’ll be watching closely in camp. And, yes, No. 7 overall pick Sonny Styles sits atop the list. We’ll write a ton about him this summer, so he gets a pass here. There are quite a few more tabs to keep moving forward. Let’s identify a few, including members of the draft class and those signed after it was complete. WR Antonio Williams Antonio Williams carries high expectations into the 2026 season, likely higher than his draft slot demands. Part of that’s out of necessity, considering the glaring hole at the No. 2 spot opposite Terry McLaurin. Scary Terry’s the other component, considering he was a third-round pick who burst onto the scene with a strong rookie season. All that pressure’s maybe a bit unfair for someone selected No. 71 overall and the ninth receiver selected, but here we are, hoping all the “draft steal” talk pans out. Williams is slippery and a top-tier separator, which should help him fit into new coordinator David Blough’s offense. I’m done hiding from it If the #Commanders don’t sign Brandon Aiyuk or Stefon Diggs, then Antonio Williams will have 800+ yards as a rookie This dude is AWESOME #RaiseHail pic.twitter.com/5R8WsNRgFz — Full Command (@FullCommandShow) July 3, 2026 It’s less important whether Williams plays inside or outside and more about whether he can build trust with quarterback Jayden Daniels in time to contribute this season. Moving from college to the NFL is a tough transition for receivers, maybe one of the toughest. The coverage is tighter and more physical, and better disguised than even guys from top programs are used to seeing. Then there’s multiple receiver positions to learn and timing to nail and unspoken communication to master. That’s, well, a lot. It’ll be interesting to see how Williams handles all that, and how the coaches adjust to find ways to help him succeed early and improve throughout the year. RB Kaytron Allen Kaytron Allen got tons of post-draft hype. That’ll happen after someone demands to be called “Fatman.” The nickname’s a fad in terms of fan interest. His Penn State highlight reel is not. The school’s all-time leading rusher can bring it, with a physical, slashing style that should play well in the pros. Flirting with the take that #Commanders RB Kaytron Allen will finish the season with 30% of the team's RB carries 4,180 yards, 39 TDs, and 5.4 YPC at Penn State is impressive. If Blough really wants Sonic and Knuckles, he's the clear Monty equivalent #RaiseHail pic.twitter.com/cyaZ3kJq0h — Full Command (@FullCommandShow) May 5, 2026 He was still available in the sixth round for a reason, though late-round running backs can make an impact. Bill Croskey-Merritt’s an example of that, a seventh-round pick who looked good right away. Allen will battle with Croskey-Merritt and veteran Rachaad White for snaps and carries. Keep an eye on Allen when the pads come on, both as a rusher and a pass protector. Snaps are hard to come by if you can’t block, and that’s a tough transition to the pros. K Drew Stevens Drew Stevens is an undrafted free agent, but Washington entered him into a position battle with Jake Moody, a former third-round pick and the first kicker taken in 2023 . The Iowa product has a big leg and an accurate one, with a career 80% field-goal success rate in college. He was at 87% as a junior and reportedly looked good during his first NFL offseason program. Kickers don’t work every day, but coaches will put Stevens in high-leverage situations whenever possible, in camp practices and preseason games, before seeing whether he can unseat Moody for the right to be the 2026 Commanders kicker. It’ll be a fun position battle to watch as the summer progresses. EDGE Joshua Josephs Joshua Josephs was the third Commanders draft pick. It also happened to come in the fifth round. Like WIlliams, that creates some confusion about what’s possible in Year 1. Josephs had a successful run at Tennessee, with 9.5 sacks and 22 tackles for a loss during his college career. His RAS falls in line with what the Commanders like, even if his listed 242 pounds seems a bit light. Joshua Josephs is light for an edge rusher, but has very good length. Good speed and explosiveness are proper starting traits, though we don't get agility testing. If agility is a concern, it was a concern for Brian Orakpo as well, but he was similarly fast and explosive. pic.twitter.com/2n49oL2nO2 — RAS.football (@MathBomb) May 3, 2026 The Commanders spent big on frontline edge rushers in Odafe Oweh and K’Lavon Chaisson but need help in the rotation. If Josephs can join that group and be productive when called upon and be a core special teams player, that’s a win. Anything beyond that is gravy. He’s another one to watch when the pads come on and, in the preseason, when he should play a ton. Flash plays are important but run defense and playing fundamental football is what earns snaps. WR Jaden Bradley Not sure if you heard, but there’s opportunity in the receiver room. That’s true higher on the depth chart and possibly on the bottom if the Commanders keep six receivers. Even that bottom spot may be tough to crack with both presumptive returners, Luke McCaffrey and Jaylin Lane, in the position group. There are two intriguing undrafted receivers in camp, with LSU’s Chris Hilton and Nevada-Las Vegas’ Jaden Bradley. We’ll focus on Bradley here, as an intriguing prospect in the mix. Head coach Dan Quinn singled Bradley out for a strong offseason program. McLaurin has mentored him a bit. Those are signs of potential identified. Bradley had a massive senior year at UNLV , with 931 yards and four touchdowns. Practice-squad spots are also coveted, and Bradley could at least earn one of those with a camp where he’s able to earn first- and second-team reps and prove capable in preseason games. That would represent a good start, much more than some catches highlighted in camp hype videos. Which rookies will you be keeping an eye on during training camp? Let us know in the comments below.
author: Scott Bair

title: Washington Commanders Camp Battles: Jerome Ford vs. Jeremy McNichols
summary: Editor’s note: We’ll be running down some key roster battles in the the leadup to Washington Commanders training camp later this month. John Portis has taken the lead on this series that will look at rookies, veterans, and free agents who are fighting for playing time in July. The Commanders backfield looks set for the […]
full_text: Editor’s note: We’ll be running down some key roster battles in the the leadup to Washington Commanders training camp later this month. John Portis has taken the lead on this series that will look at rookies, veterans, and free agents who are fighting for playing time in July. The Commanders backfield looks set for the first three slots on the depth chart headed into camp. While the order is yet to be determined, Bill Croskey-Merritt, Rachaad White, and rookie Kaytron Allen all appear poised to secure spots on the roster with a good camp and preseason. Behind them, one of the better roster battles of training camp is brewing between Jerome Ford and Jeremy McNichols . Ford was drafted in the fifth round of the 2022 NFL Draft by the Cleveland Browns. After going on injured reserve early in his rookie season, Ford would get a lot of run in 2023 after Nick Chubb tore his ACL. Ford acquitted himself well, finishing the season with 813 rushing yards and four touchdowns on 204 rushing attempts, as well as 44 catches for 319 yards and five touchdowns on 63 targets. Ford was named the starter headed into 2024 but was replaced by Chubb when healthy and relegated to third-down duties in 2025. Washington fans can’t help but look at his 4.3 yards-per-carry average along with his highlight reels and get excited about what he may add to the backfield as a change-of-pace back for the Commanders. From a roster standpoint, Ford may not be as appealing. While his numbers in a relief role look good, his inefficiency shows up when given multiple carries. Jerome’s poor vision results in frequent tackles for a loss or minimal gains. His efficiency in 2023 ranks closely to another current Commanders running back, one poorly regarded for his rushing ability. Running Back Efficiency – Through Week 14 pic.twitter.com/eJZ1YGJ65K — SūmerSports (@SumerSports) December 12, 2023 Ford also doesn’t offer much in the way of special teams, historically playing less than ten percent of the Browns’ special teams stats. Ford’s history indicates his role would appear to be more of a change-of-pace option instead of a reliable backup and special teamer. Meanwhile, efficiency and special teams are a hallmark of Ford’s competition. Also drafted in the fifth round by the Buccaneers, McNichols joined the NFL in 2017. The Boise State product was a fringe/practice squad player for years , with the notable exception on his second stint with the Titans. Upon arriving in Washington, McNichols was earmarked for the practice squad by many fans, but impressed the coaching staff. His versatility won him a roster spot. He was used effectively in a rotation in 2024, and stepped in admirably after Austin Ekeler’s departure last season, where he made the most of his limited carries and receptions. Jeremy McNichols' ability to move the chains is just crazy. On 44 rushes, 13 went for 1st downs. On 25 catches, 10 went for 1st downs. 23 1st downs on 69 touches. 1 out of every 3 touches was a 1st down! pic.twitter.com/wsuqbQd7kI — JP Finlay (@JPFinlayNBCS) July 20, 2026 A plus special teamer and protector, McNichols played on 53% the Commanders special teams snaps in 2024, but only 14% last season when he was more heavily involved in the running back rotation. So far, in offseason activities, Ford has caught the eye of the staff and media, with team beat writer Zach Selby noting he “continues to run hard and look impressive as a pass-catcher.” Meanwhile, McNichols has shown up ready to go for another season and has also caught Selby’s attention. Jeremy McNichols might be one of the older active players on the roster, but the 30-year-old running back still has some quickness to him. He’s looked impressive running team drills throughout OTAs as both a ball carrier and pass catcher. He managed to avoid getting touched by defenders during seven-on-seven drills, juking multiple defenders near the right sideline. Both players appear ready to bring their all to the competition for the last roster spot in the running back room, but just beating out the other man might not be enough. There are several areas on the roster where an additional spot might be needed and with three versatile players projected in the running back room, Washington might opt to only carry three running backs this year. The idea would be at least one of Ford or McNichols would be available to sign to the practice squad, with the possible addition of Robert Henry Jr . there as well. Will the running backs make a case for the need to carry a fourth player at the position? If so, will Ford or McNichols be that player? Jerome Ford runs 62 yards for the TD! 📺: #KCvsCLE on CBS/Paramount+ 📱: https://t.co/waVpO909ge pic.twitter.com/SUozPWSvm1 — NFL (@NFL) December 15, 2024 Vs. Jeremy McNichols bounces off tackles for the 60-yard TD! LVvsWAS on FOX/FOX One https://t.co/HkKw7uXVnt pic.twitter.com/x8j0UTgN2I — NFL (@NFL) September 21, 2025

title: Commanders News – Okonkwo, Williams & Burks: Enough help for Daniels?
summary: The Daily Slop – 24 July 2026 Editor’s note: Each day, Hogs Haven compiles a collection of articles, podcasts & tweets from around the web to keep you in touch with the Commanders, the NFC East, the NFL and sports in general, with a sprinkling of other stuff. Enjoy! Commanders links Articles Sports Illustrated Chig […]
full_text: Nov 30, 2025; Landover, Maryland, USA; Washington Commanders wide receiver Treylon Burks (13) makes a catch for a touchdown defended by Denver Broncos cornerback Riley Moss (21) in the third quarter of the game at Northwest Stadium. Mandatory Credit: Peter Casey-Imagn Images | Peter Casey-Imagn Images The Daily Slop – 24 July 2026 Editor’s note: Each day, Hogs Haven compiles a collection of articles, podcasts & tweets from around the web to keep you in touch with the Commanders, the NFC East, the NFL and sports in general, with a sprinkling of other stuff. Enjoy! Commanders links Articles Sports Illustrated Chig Okonkwo gives Jayden Daniels a more dynamic receiving threat, allowing Bates and Sinnott to settle into clearer roles When Zach Ertz went down in Week 14 last season after taking a hit to his right knee, fans’ worst fears were confirmed almost immediately. A Washington Commanders campaign that was already tainted by a relentless slew of injuries added another notable name to the IR in their veteran tight end, who’d see his second straight season with at least 50 receptions prematurely end at the hands of a torn ACL. The loss of his presence as star quarterback Jayden Daniels’ most comfortable go-to short-area target was stark over the last four weeks of the disappointing winter, especially when his understudies were unable to fill the pass-catching vacuum he’d left behind. As helpful as John Bates’ blocking was , and with as much as third-stringer Ben Sinnott stands to prove, Washington’s front office readied for a pressure-filled offseason where they’d have to find someone to balance out the Commanders’ offense. Enter Chig Okonkwo. The former University of Maryland standout is on the move for the first time since getting drafted by the Tennessee Titans four years ago, and as a free-agent addition, he’ll step right into Ertz’s former role as the top receiving option within the positional depth chart . His impact will stretch well beyond what he’s able to do at the individual level as one of Daniels’ newest targets ; with Okonkwo’s added flavor, the returning supplementary contributors at tight end have the chance to surge in settling into their own niches. While Okonkwo left a few of his most ardent believers disappointed with his inability to look like a star next to Tennessee’s No. 1 drafted quarterback in Cam Ward, especially given the rookie’s usual willingness to lean on hitting checkdown targets, he did what Ertz couldn’t in making plays happen after the catch. His 6.1 yards after the catch per reception in 2025 were his most since his rookie season, and he did that while setting career highs in targets (79) and receptions (56). The physical 26-year-old is much more dynamic than your average replacement-level, catch-first tight end. He should be able to hold his own on the blocking end and stands to thrive in space as one of Daniels’ top receiving options behind Terry McLaurin. To read more of this article, CLICK HERE NOTUS.com Five Players to Watch at Commanders Training Camp For all the chatter about the Commanders needing another receiver ahead of training camp, it seems pretty clear they’re rolling with what they currently have. Which means someone has to line up opposite McLaurin, and it would appear Williams, a 2026 third-round pick, and Burks, a 2022 first-rounder in Tennessee, have the upper hand. During 7-on-7 and 11-on-11 drills at OTAs and minicamp, Williams and Burks got a lot of time working with quarterbacks Daniels and Marcus Mariota. Williams was primarily used out of the slot at Clemson last season, and his production didn’t exactly scream modern NFL starter (55 receptions, 604 yards, 11.0 yards per reception). But he is versatile and slippery, often used in jet sweeps and screens that take advantage of his speed. Much like most of the rest of the receiving corps, Williams is not a deep threat, but he can feast on defenses in intermediate routes. Injuries have derailed Burks’ career, limiting him to just 35 games played in the last four years. But he’s shown big-play ability , albeit in spurts. If Williams can find gaps in coverage and Burks can stay healthy, there’s a good chance one of them will earn a starting spot by the end of camp. This — and the elevation of WSH’s receivers in the Blough scheme via shifts and motions — gives me hope that their… — Grant Paulsen (@GrantPaulsen) July 24, 2026 From Commanders Roundtable : Selected 71st overall out of Clemson, [Antonio] Williams’ primary strength lies in his route-running nuance and ability to create separation. Williams stood out as a college junior, compiling 904 yards and 11 touchdowns on 75 catches while displaying elite short-area quickness and spatial awareness. However, his senior season was plagued by minor injuries and inconsistent quarterback play. That production dip allowed Williams to slip to the third round—which could end up being a major steal for Washington if things break right. Williams’ disciplined route-running should fit like a glove in David Blough’s structured system. The Scheme Fit: Blough’s offense borrows heavily from the Detroit Lions’ system, where Blough spent time as a backup quarterback under Ben Johnson. That system famously weaponizes route technicians who can win inside the slot and flex outside. The Stumbling Block: He’s a rookie. While analysts have drawn comparisons to Amon-Ra St. Brown due to his frame and route precision, Williams must quickly prove he can handle the physical demands of the NFL and showcase true scheme versatility both in the slot and on the perimeter. If Williams hits the ground running in August, he gives Washington an organic, high-upside WR2 who can win at all three levels. The Case for Burks: He gives Jayden Daniels a true “big-bodied” target on the boundary. In 50/50 ball situations and red-zone packages, Burks provides a physical presence that complements McLaurin’s speed. The Red Flag: Durability and consistency. Burks has flashed elite potential in spurts, but he must prove he can stay healthy across a full training camp workload and absorb Blough’s playbook without hesitation. He also needs to get acclimated to David Blough’s offense, which will see Daniels taking snaps under center far more now that his former assistant QB coach is his offensive coordinator after two seasons with Kliff Kingsbury in that role. Daniels is also in the latest season of Netflix’s Quarterback series. All eyes and a heap of responsibility will be on Daniels. title: Washington Commanders 92-man 2026 pre-training camp roster/depth chart
summary: Reviewing the roster limit As you are probably aware, the NFL CBA allows each team to have 90 players on its offseason roster, but it also makes provisions for a 91st player who joins the team via the International Player Pathway (IPP) program. For the last several years, the Commanders have made use of this […]
full_text: Reviewing the roster limit As you are probably aware, the NFL CBA allows each team to have 90 players on its offseason roster, but it also makes provisions for a 91st player who joins the team via the International Player Pathway (IPP) program. For the last several years, the Commanders have made use of this IPP exemption, as they have again this season, so Washington’s offseason roster limit is once again 91 players. Washington’s 91st player via the IPP is currently edge rusher TJ Maguranyanga , who spent the 2025 season with the Commanders as well. An unanswered question As the Commanders head into training camp, with rookies reporting to camp Friday (July 24) and veterans reporting on Tuesday, there is at least one outstanding roster question to be resolved. It was recently and widely reported by sports media that Washington had signed veteran cornerback Rasul Douglas . This signing was also reported by the team , but the Commanders website hasn’t added the cornerback’s name to the roster page . Without Douglas’ name on the roster, Washington’s team site lists 91 players. Our Lads does have Douglas included on their depth chart, but it lists 92 players. The signing of Douglas appears on the official NFL transactions list on July 6, but there is no corresponding roster move to make space for him on the roster. Right now, without more information, it looks like the Commanders have 92 players, which is one player too many. It appears as if another transaction will need to happen (or be announced) soon to keep the Commanders in compliance with the 91-man training camp roster limit. That transaction could be the release of a player, but it could also result from a player being placed on the PUP (Physically Unable to Perform) list or other reserve list that removes him, usually temporarily, from being counted against the roster limit. I expect that roster transaction to be announced by Tuesday. In the meantime, since I don’t know what the team will do to create the roster opening, I’m presenting a 92-man depth chart here. So, before this article was even published, it was out of date — someone on the chart below will not be a full participant in next week’s training camp, and may not be on the roster this time next week. Changes since the last iteration of the depth chart Since the last time I published a depth chart article , there have been just a few changes: WR Ja’Corey Brooks was cut TE Anthony Firsker was signed Also, as mentioned above, CB Rasul Douglas has reportedly agreed to terms with the team, but no corresponding roster move to open a roster spot for him has been announced, nor does the NFL transaction wire list any such transaction. As a result, we should expect at least one more roster transaction in the coming days. Not your typical depth chart The chart below is only a depth chart insofar as it assigns players to positions and stacks them in an order. The primary purpose of the chart is to keep track of the 92 guys that currently comprise the training camp roster, not to predict gameday alignments. You will note, for example, that I have 12 offensive positions and 13 defensive positions on the chart, despite the fact that a team can only field 11 players at one time. You will also note that each player’s name appears only once regardless of the fact that he may play in multiple alignments or positions ( e.g., an interior offensive lineman who can play center and both guard spots will appear at only one of those positions, not all of them ). Again, this is by design since the goal is to provide handy visual reference of the 92 individual players while also offering an overall snapshot of team strength and depth. The bias, though, is to provide a visual list of the full roster, not so much to create a game-ready depth chart. Finally, you will also note that, where players are capable of playing more than one position (and likely to do so on game days), my decision on where to align them may be very different from your idea of where they belong. Here are comments on a couple of players who may seem misaligned to you: Antonio Williams I don’t think any informed fan will argue against the idea that this year’s third-round draft pick will play both inside (slot) and outside on offense. Because he played primarily in the slot in his final year at Clemson in 2025 , many people insist that he will be Washington’s primary slot receiver in 2026. I have repeatedly pointed to Adam Peters’ comments all offseason about Williams’ play outside in 2024 and his abilities as a wideout as one reason for my belief that the Clemson product is seen by the Commanders front office and coaching staff as a solution to the seeming need for a receiver to play opposite McLaurin. In addition, the team already has Luke McCaffrey and Jaylin Lane — a pair of recently drafted players with inside/outside skills — available for the slot. Further, we have heard multiple indications that the Commanders will play more 12 and 13 personnel this season, which would take one WR off the field. When that happens, I expect McLaurin and Williams to be the first choice to remain on the field in multiple tight end sets, most likely boosting the number of snaps Williams lines up on the outside. In my mind, all of this adds up to Williams aligning wide more than in the slot — which, by the way, would be consistent with the Lions’ use of Amon-Ra St. Brown, who is a frequent comp for Washington’s plans for AW: For all these reasons, I have listed Williams on the chart as the primary receiver opposite McLaurin. My chart would change in an instant if, for example, the team signed Stefon Diggs on Monday. Mike Sainristil I don’t think all the questions about the cornerback room are settled. I don’t think we know if Trey Amos is fully healthy. I don’t think we know whether Rasul Douglas was signed in the expectation of him starting or simply providing depth. I don’t think we know whether Mike Sainristil will end up as a starter or a backup, or whether he will align primarily as a wide corner or slot defender. In a manner similar to the increased use of tight ends on offense, the expected increase in three-safety looks on defense this season could lead to more alignments with only two 2 cornerbacks on the field instead of traditional nickel schemes. I have chosen, in the chart below, to assume that Amos will be healthy, that Douglas will be the primary CB on the opposite side, and that Sainristil will be the primary backup at both slot and out wide. I have listed him behind Amik Robertson on the chart. Of course, training camp and preseason could totally rewrite my ideas about how the secondary will be deployed. Consider these thoughts, published by A to Z Sports earlier this week: There are rumblings that the Commanders want to move Quan Martin into the primary nickel role, and honestly, that doesn’t make much sense to me. The majority of the safeties on the roster lack range, and Amik Robinson is a perfectly capable inside player. If Martin does slide to nickel, that leaves two cornerbacks under 5-foot-10 starting on the outside in both [Robertson] and Sainristill. And while both guys have shown they can play bigger than their body size, you don’t want your starting outside corners to both be under 5-foot-11. The Commanders could easily make a big mistake here and set themselves up in a bad spot by not only depriving themselves of their most capable centerfielder, but exposing the perimeter, as well. I have not included cap hits below $1.5m. The Commanders currently have 45 defensive players, 43 offensive players and 4 special teams players.
